# Overview

In Exercise 6, regions were built from several variables measured over townships. Exercise 9 is
about one variable, the resale price of a condominium unit, and about whether the effect of each
feature of a unit on its price is the same everywhere in Singapore. Two units with the same floor
area, age and tenure sell for different prices in different places. The questions on slides 3 and 4
are why some units sold at higher prices than others, and why units in the central part of the
island sold at higher prices.

Why some units sold at higher prices than others is examined with a hedonic pricing model, one
regression for the whole island. Why central units sold at higher prices is examined with a
geographically weighted regression (GWR). GWR fits a separate regression at every transaction, from
the transactions near that transaction, so that each coefficient may differ from place to place.

**Part 1** is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 13: the data, exploratory analysis, a simple and a
multiple linear regression with their diagnostics, a test of the residuals for spatial
autocorrelation, and GWR with a fixed and an adaptive bandwidth. In **Part 2**, the chapter's method
is compared with the Lesson 9 slides and readings. The analysis is then extended with the tests and
maps described in the readings.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

## Sources

The hands-on exercise is one chapter, assigned for Lesson 9:

- [Chapter 13: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR
  Method](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap13.html)

Two papers are set as self-reading on the Lesson 9 outline.

| Reading                                                                                              | What it contributes                                                                                                                                                                          | Used in               |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1996)**, "Geographically Weighted Regression: A Method for Exploring Spatial Nonstationarity" | GWR as local weighted least squares, the Gaussian and bisquare kernels, the CV score for the bandwidth, and Monte Carlo tests of whether the coefficients vary                              | 3.3, 4.3, 4.6         |
| **Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1999)**, "Some Notes on Parametric Significance Tests for Geographically Weighted Regression" | the ANOVA comparing GWR with OLS, and mixed GWR, in which some coefficients are global | 4.6                   |

On the outline, the GWR paper of Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton is dated 2002, with pages
281-289. The paper was published in *Geographical Analysis* 28(4), October 1996, on pages 281
to 298. The paper is cited as 1996 on this page.

The outline also lists two references, Mennis (2006) and Matthews and Yang (2012). Both are used:

| Reference                                                                                                 | What it contributes                                                                                                         | Used in |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------|
| **Mennis (2006)**, "Mapping the Results of Geographically Weighted Regression"                              | Coefficients mapped together with their t-values, with a diverging colour scheme centred on zero                             | 4.7     |
| **Matthews and Yang (2012)**, "Mapping the results of local statistics: Using geographically weighted regression" | Only the significant coefficients shown, on one map; the Byrne, Charlton and Fotheringham (2009) adjustment for multiple tests | 4.7     |

From the "All About R" section of the outline, two `GWmodel` papers are used. Gollini et al. (2015,
section 7) is used for local collinearity, in section 4.4 of this page. Lu et al. (2014) is used for
the Monte Carlo test (section 4.2 of the paper), local collinearity diagnostics (section 5.2 of the
paper) and the adjustment of local p-values (section 5.1 of the paper). The outline's other
packages, `spgwr`, `gwrr` and `lctools`, are not used.

The slide numbers on this page were first taken from last year's deck, dated 13 September 2025.
This year's Lesson 9 deck, published on 27 October 2026, has the same 39 slides in the same order.

:::

# Getting started

## Packages

```{r}
pacman::p_load(olsrr, corrplot, ggpubr, sf, sfdep, spdep, GWmodel, tmap,
               tidyverse, gtsummary, performance, see, RColorBrewer, lmtest,
               patchwork, knitr)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
step_fill <- c(added = "#c8ecc8", removed = "#f6c6c6", changed = "#ffe8a3")
step_table <- function(d, title, added = NULL, removed = NULL, changed = NULL, cells = NULL,
                       left = NULL) {
  css <- function(col, i = 0) {
    f <- if (any(cells$row == i & cells$col == col)) step_fill[["changed"]]
         else if (col %in% added) step_fill[["added"]]
         else if (col %in% removed) step_fill[["removed"]]
         else if (col %in% changed) step_fill[["changed"]]
    paste0("padding: 2px 6px; border: 1px solid #bbb; white-space: nowrap; text-align: ",
           if (col %in% left) "left;" else "right;",
           " box-shadow: none;", if (!is.null(f)) paste0(" background: ", f, ";"))
  }
  htmltools::tags$div(
    htmltools::tags$div(style = "font-size: 0.85em; margin-bottom: 3px;", htmltools::HTML(title)),
    htmltools::tags$table(
      style = "border-collapse: collapse; font-size: 0.8em;",
      htmltools::tags$tr(lapply(names(d), \(n) htmltools::tags$th(style = css(n), n))),
      lapply(seq_len(nrow(d)), \(i) htmltools::tags$tr(
        lapply(names(d), \(n) htmltools::tags$td(style = css(n, i), d[[n]][i]))))))
}
show_steps <- function(...) {
  tables <- list(...)
  arrow <- htmltools::tags$div(style = "font-size: 1.5em; color: #888; padding-top: 0.7em;", "→")
  items <- c(tables[1], lapply(tables[-1], \(t) htmltools::tags$div(
    style = "display: flex; gap: 0.6em; align-items: flex-start;", arrow, t)))
  htmltools::tags$div(style = "display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.6em; margin: 0.4em 0;", items)
}
fmt_n <- function(x, d = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pt_text <- function(g, d) {
  xy <- sf::st_coordinates(g)
  sprintf("POINT (%s %s)", formatC(xy[, 1], format = "f", digits = d),
          formatC(xy[, 2], format = "f", digits = d))
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
pacman::p_load(...)                                       # pacman
```

- `p_load()` installs any package that is missing and then attaches all of them, so one call
  replaces a series of `install.packages()` and `library()` calls.

| Package                  | Used for                                                                  |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `sf`                     | reading the subzones, converting the transactions to points              |
| `tidyverse`              | reading and reshaping the transaction table, `ggplot2` charts              |
| `ggpubr`, `patchwork`    | arranging several charts in one figure                                     |
| `corrplot`               | the correlation matrix of the explanatory variables                        |
| `gtsummary`              | the regression table                                                       |
| `performance`, `see`     | the collinearity, linearity and normality checks, with plots              |
| `olsrr`                  | a residual plot (named in the chapter's package list)                      |
| `sfdep`, `spdep`         | distance-band neighbours, Moran's I of the residuals                       |
| `GWmodel`                | bandwidth selection, geographically weighted regression                    |
| `tmap`, `RColorBrewer`   | point maps, colour palettes                                                |
| `lmtest`                 | the Breusch-Pagan test (Part 2)                                            |
| `knitr`                  | formatting tables computed on the page                                     |

The chapter's package list includes `olsrr`, and the chapter runs the diagnostics with
`performance`. Both `olsrr` and `performance` are loaded here. In section 3.2.7, one plot is drawn
with each package. `spdep`, `lmtest`, `patchwork` and `knitr` are additions to the chapter's list.
`see` draws the plots of `performance`, and the chapter's `plot()` calls load it without naming it.
:::

## The data

The two data files of section 13.2 were taken from Dr. Kam's AY2025-26 course repository
(`In-class_Ex/In-class_Ex07/data`). With these files, the numbers printed in the chapter are
reproduced below, among them the slope of 14,719 and R² of 0.4518 in section 3.2.1, the bandwidths
of 971.3405 m and 30 neighbours, and the AICc values of 42263.61 and 41982.22 in section 3.3.

| Layer                  | Format         | Features      | Native CRS                         | Contents                                                     |
|------------------------|----------------|---------------|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL`  | ESRI shapefile | 323 polygons  | SVY21, without an EPSG code         | URA Master Plan 2014 planning subzones                        |
| `Condo_resale_2015`    | CSV            | 1,436 rows    | WGS 84 longitude and latitude       | Condominium resale transactions in 2015, 23 fields            |

### Planning subzone boundaries

```{r}
#| results: hide
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL")
```

```{r}
mpsz_svy21 <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
st_crs(mpsz_svy21)$epsg
st_bbox(mpsz_svy21)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses four functions:

```r
st_read(dsn, layer)                                       # sf
st_transform(x, crs)                                      # sf
st_crs(x)                                                 # sf
st_bbox(obj)                                              # sf
```

- `st_read()` reads the shapefile into an sf data frame of 323 subzones. It prints a summary that
  begins with the full path of the data folder on the computer that renders the page. The chunk
  option `results: hide` keeps that summary off the page.
- `st_transform(mpsz, 3414)` attaches EPSG:3414, the code for SVY21 / Singapore TM. The `.prj` file
  describes the same projection without the code, so the transformation leaves every coordinate
  unchanged. The largest difference from `st_set_crs(mpsz, 3414)` is 0 m.
- `st_crs()$epsg` returns the code, which is 3414 after the transformation.
- `st_bbox()` returns the extent of the layer in metres.

**Example** (first two rows):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_x <- function(x) sapply(st_geometry(x)[1:2], \(g) st_coordinates(g)[1, 1])
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(SUBZONE_N = mpsz$SUBZONE_N[1:2], x = fmt_n(stp_x(mpsz), 1), EPSG = "none"),
             "<code>mpsz</code>", changed = "EPSG"),
  step_table(tibble(SUBZONE_N = mpsz_svy21$SUBZONE_N[1:2], x = fmt_n(stp_x(mpsz_svy21), 1),
                    EPSG = "3414"),
             "<code>mpsz_svy21</code>", changed = "EPSG"))
```

`x` is the first corner of each subzone boundary, in metres. Only the EPSG code changes.
:::

### Condominium resale transactions

```{r}
condo_resale <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Condo_resale_2015.csv")
glimpse(condo_resale)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
read_csv(file)                                            # readr
glimpse(x)                                                # dplyr
```

- `read_csv()` reads the file into a tibble of 1,436 rows, one per transaction.
- `glimpse()` prints one line per column with its type and first values.
:::

The 23 columns are in four groups:

| Group                     | Columns                                                                                     |
|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| location                  | `LATITUDE`, `LONGITUDE`, `POSTCODE`                                                         |
| price, the response       | `SELLING_PRICE`, in Singapore dollars                                                       |
| the unit and its project  | `AREA_SQM`, `AGE` (years), `NO_Of_UNITS`, `FAMILY_FRIENDLY`, `FREEHOLD`, `LEASEHOLD_99YR`   |
| distance to amenities     | 13 columns named `PROX_...`, in kilometres                                                  |

`FAMILY_FRIENDLY`, `FREEHOLD` and `LEASEHOLD_99YR` are 0 or 1. In the chapter's text,
`LEASEHOLD_99YR` is called `LEASE_99YEAR`, a name that is not in the file.

```{r}
summary(condo_resale[, c("SELLING_PRICE", "AREA_SQM", "AGE", "PROX_CBD", "PROX_MRT")])
```

### Transactions as points

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- st_as_sf(condo_resale,
                            coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
                            crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
```

```{r}
n_dup <- sum(duplicated(st_coordinates(condo_resale.sf)))
n_dup
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
st_as_sf(x, coords, crs)                                  # sf
st_coordinates(x)                                         # sf
duplicated(x)                                             # base R
```

- `st_as_sf()` builds a point from the two coordinate columns of each row. `coords` lists the x
  column first, so longitude comes before latitude. `crs = 4326` declares the coordinates as WGS 84
  degrees.
- `st_transform(crs = 3414)` projects the points to SVY21, the CRS of the subzones, so that
  distances between points are in metres.
- `st_coordinates()` returns the x and y of each point. `duplicated()` marks every row whose
  coordinates occur in an earlier row.

**Example** (first two rows):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_0 <- condo_resale[1:2, ]
stp_1 <- st_as_sf(stp_0, coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4326)
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(POSTCODE = stp_0$POSTCODE, LONGITUDE = fmt_n(stp_0$LONGITUDE, 5),
                    LATITUDE = fmt_n(stp_0$LATITUDE, 5)),
             "<code>condo_resale</code>", removed = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE")),
  step_table(tibble(POSTCODE = stp_1$POSTCODE, geometry = pt_text(stp_1, 5)),
             "<code>st_as_sf()</code>", added = "geometry"),
  step_table(tibble(POSTCODE = stp_1$POSTCODE, geometry = pt_text(condo_resale.sf[1:2, ], 0)),
             "<code>st_transform()</code>", changed = "geometry"))
```

`st_as_sf()` replaces the two coordinate columns with one point in degrees. `st_transform()` then
converts the point to metres, the unit of SVY21. The other columns are kept and not shown.

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_xy <- st_coordinates(condo_resale.sf)[98:99, ]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(row = 98:99, POSTCODE = condo_resale.sf$POSTCODE[98:99],
                    x = fmt_n(stp_xy[, 1], 1), y = fmt_n(stp_xy[, 2], 1),
                    `duplicated()` = as.character(duplicated(st_coordinates(condo_resale.sf))[98:99])),
             "Rows 98 and 99: same point", added = "duplicated()"))
```
:::

In the data, `r n_dup` transactions share their coordinates with an earlier transaction. Every row
has its own postcode, and rows at the same point have nearby postcodes, such as 425562 and 425602
in rows 98 and 99. Each row is a separate transaction, so every transaction is kept.

# Part 1: Chapter 13

## Exploratory data analysis

### Distribution of the selling price

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = SELLING_PRICE)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, colour = "black", fill = "light blue")
```

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf |>
  mutate(LOG_SELLING_PRICE = log(SELLING_PRICE))
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = LOG_SELLING_PRICE)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, colour = "black", fill = "light blue")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
ggplot(data, aes(x))                                      # ggplot2
geom_histogram(bins, colour, fill)                        # ggplot2
mutate(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
```

- `geom_histogram(bins = 20)` divides the range of the price into 20 intervals of equal width and
  draws a bar for the number of transactions in each interval.
- `mutate()` adds the column `LOG_SELLING_PRICE`, the natural logarithm of the price.

**Example** (first two rows):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_p <- condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE[1:2]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(SELLING_PRICE = fmt_n(stp_p),
                    LOG_SELLING_PRICE = sprintf("log(%s) = %s", fmt_n(stp_p),
                                                fmt_n(log(stp_p), 3))),
             "<code>mutate()</code>", added = "LOG_SELLING_PRICE"))
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
skew <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
skew_price <- skew(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE)
skew_log <- skew(condo_resale.sf$LOG_SELLING_PRICE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
price_q <- scales::dollar(quantile(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE, c(0.25, 0.75)))
price_max <- scales::dollar(max(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE))
```

The prices are skewed to the right: half the units sold for between `r price_q[1]`
and `r price_q[2]`, the first and third quartiles. The highest price is `r price_max`. The skewness
is `r round(skew_price, 2)` on the dollar scale and `r round(skew_log, 2)` on the log scale. In the
chapter, `LOG_SELLING_PRICE` is computed and then every model is built on `SELLING_PRICE`. In Part
1, the models are fitted on `SELLING_PRICE`, as in the chapter. In section 4.1, they are fitted on
the log scale.

### Distributions of the explanatory variables

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
hist_vars <- c("AREA_SQM", "AGE", "PROX_CBD", "PROX_CHILDCARE",
               "PROX_ELDERLYCARE", "PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA", "PROX_HAWKER_MARKET",
               "PROX_KINDERGARTEN", "PROX_MRT", "PROX_PARK",
               "PROX_PRIMARY_SCH", "PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH")
hist_plots <- map(hist_vars, \(v)
  ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, colour = "black", fill = "light blue"))
ggarrange(plotlist = hist_plots, ncol = 3, nrow = 4)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
map(.x, .f)                                               # purrr
ggarrange(plotlist, ncol, nrow)                           # ggpubr
```

- The chapter writes out the same `ggplot()` call twelve times, once per variable. `map()` runs it
  once for each name in `hist_vars` and returns the twelve charts as a list. `.data[[v]]` picks the
  column whose name is held in `v`.
- `ggarrange(plotlist = ...)` places the twelve charts in a grid of 3 columns and 4 rows.

**Example**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_v <- hist_vars[c(1, 2, 12)]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(v = stp_v,
                    `.data[[v]]` = sapply(stp_v, \(v)
                      paste(fmt_n(head(condo_resale.sf[[v]], 3), 2), collapse = ", ")),
                    hist_plots = c("[[1]] chart", "[[2]] chart", "[[12]] chart")) |>
               add_row(v = "...", `.data[[v]]` = "...", hist_plots = "...", .before = 3),
             "<code>map()</code>: one chart per name", added = "hist_plots"),
  step_table(tibble(`column 1` = hist_vars[c(1, 4, 7, 10)], `column 2` = hist_vars[c(2, 5, 8, 11)],
                    `column 3` = hist_vars[c(3, 6, 9, 12)]),
             "<code>ggarrange(ncol = 3, nrow = 4)</code>"))
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
x_skew <- sapply(st_drop_geometry(condo_resale.sf)[hist_vars], skew)
```

Of the 12 variables, `r sum(x_skew > 1)` have a skewness above 1, like the price. For the distance
variables, most units are close to an amenity of the kind measured and a few are far from one. The
skewness of `PROX_CHILDCARE` is `r round(x_skew["PROX_CHILDCARE"], 1)`. The skewness of `AREA_SQM`,
`PROX_MRT` and `PROX_PRIMARY_SCH` is about 2. `PROX_CBD` (`r round(x_skew["PROX_CBD"], 2)`) and
`PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA` (`r round(x_skew["PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA"], 2)`) are close to symmetric.

### Point map of the selling prices

```{r}
tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "SELLING_PRICE",
          fill_alpha = 0.6,
          size = 0.5,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile")) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11, 14))
tmap_mode("plot")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses five functions:

```r
tmap_mode(mode)                                           # tmap
tm_shape(shp) + tm_polygons()                             # tmap
tm_dots(fill, fill_alpha, size, fill.scale)               # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(style)                                 # tmap
tm_view(set_zoom_limits)                                  # tmap
```

- `tmap_mode("view")` draws the next maps as interactive web maps. `tmap_mode("plot")` returns to
  static maps.
- `tm_dots()` draws one dot per transaction, coloured by `SELLING_PRICE`, at 60% opacity.
- `tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile")` divides the prices into classes that hold the same number
  of transactions.
- `set_zoom_limits = c(11, 14)` keeps the zoom level between 11, the whole island, and 14, a few
  streets.

**Example**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_brk <- classInt::classIntervals(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE, n = 5, style = "quantile")$brks
stp_cls <- cut(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE, stp_brk, include.lowest = TRUE)
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(class = 1:5,
                    `SELLING_PRICE` = paste(scales::dollar(head(stp_brk, -1)), "to",
                                            scales::dollar(stp_brk[-1])),
                    transactions = as.vector(table(stp_cls))),
             "<code>style = \"quantile\"</code>: five classes", added = "transactions"))
```

The counts differ slightly because several units sold at exactly the price of a break.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
condo_pa <- st_join(condo_resale.sf, mpsz_svy21[, c("PLN_AREA_N", "REGION_N")])
q_price <- quantile(condo_pa$SELLING_PRICE, c(0.2, 0.8))
top_fifth <- condo_pa |> filter(SELLING_PRICE >= q_price[2])
low_fifth <- condo_pa |> filter(SELLING_PRICE <= q_price[1])
top_pa <- sort(table(top_fifth$PLN_AREA_N), decreasing = TRUE)
low_pa <- sort(table(low_fifth$PLN_AREA_N), decreasing = TRUE)
low_reg <- table(low_fifth$REGION_N)
```

Of the `r nrow(top_fifth)` units in the most expensive
fifth, `r sum(top_fifth$REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")` are in the Central Region, with the largest
numbers in Bukit Timah (`r top_pa["BUKIT TIMAH"]`), Tanglin (`r top_pa["TANGLIN"]`) and River Valley
(`r top_pa["RIVER VALLEY"]`). Of the `r nrow(low_fifth)` units in the cheapest
fifth, `r sum(low_fifth$REGION_N != "CENTRAL REGION")` are in the East (`r low_reg["EAST REGION"]`),
North (`r low_reg["NORTH REGION"]`), West (`r low_reg["WEST REGION"]`) and North-East
(`r low_reg["NORTH-EAST REGION"]`) Regions, most often in Tampines (`r low_pa["TAMPINES"]`), Bedok
(`r low_pa["BEDOK"]`) and Pasir Ris (`r low_pa["PASIR RIS"]`) in the east, and Yishun
(`r low_pa["YISHUN"]`) and Woodlands (`r low_pa["WOODLANDS"]`) in the north.

## Hedonic pricing with linear regression

::: callout-note
## What a hedonic pricing model is

A home has features: floor area, age, tenure, and distance to the city centre, a station, a park or
a school. In a hedonic pricing model, the price is the sum of the values of the home's features. The
regression estimates the value of each feature. In the chapter, the coefficient of `AREA_SQM` is the
price of one more square metre. The coefficient of `PROX_MRT` is the change in price for each extra
kilometre from the nearest MRT station.

According to section 13.1, the chapter's features are structural or locational:

- **structural**: floor area, age, number of units in the development, family-friendly status,
  freehold status;
- **locational**: distance to the CBD and to amenities such as MRT stations, parks and schools.
:::

### Simple linear regression

```{r}
condo.slr <- lm(formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM,
                data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.slr)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
lm(formula, data)                                         # stats
summary(object)                                           # base R
```

- `lm()` fits a straight line by least squares. The formula `SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM` names the
  response on the left of `~` and the explanatory variable on the right.
- `summary()` prints the coefficients with their standard errors, t-values and p-values, then R²,
  adjusted R² and the F test.
:::

The fitted line is

$$\widehat{\text{price}} = `r format(round(coef(condo.slr)[1], 1), big.mark = ",")` + `r format(round(coef(condo.slr)[2], 1), big.mark = ",")` \times \text{area (m}^2\text{)}$$

so each extra square metre adds about `r scales::dollar(round(coef(condo.slr)[2]))` to the price.
The negative intercept is the price of a unit of zero area. The smallest unit in the data
has `r min(condo_resale.sf$AREA_SQM)` m², so the intercept is an extrapolation without a practical
interpretation. R² is `r round(summary(condo.slr)$r.squared, 4)`: the floor area accounts
for `r round(100 * summary(condo.slr)$r.squared)`% of the variation in price. In the chapter, the
same number is read as explaining "about 45% of the resale prices". R² is a share of the variation
of the price around its mean.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = AREA_SQM, y = SELLING_PRICE)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
geom_point()                                              # ggplot2
geom_smooth(method = lm)                                  # ggplot2
```

- `geom_smooth(method = lm)` fits the same least-squares line as `lm()`. It draws the line with a
  grey band, the 95% confidence interval of the mean price at each value of area.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
slr_res <- residuals(condo.slr)
big_area <- condo_resale.sf$AREA_SQM >= 200
```

In all, `r sum(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE > 1e7)` transactions sold for more than 10 million
dollars, the highest for `r scales::dollar(max(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE))`
with `r condo_resale.sf$AREA_SQM[which.max(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE)]` m². The standard
deviation of the residuals is `r scales::dollar(round(sd(slr_res[!big_area]), -3))` for units below
200 m² and `r scales::dollar(round(sd(slr_res[big_area]), -3))` for larger units.

::: callout-note
## How least squares fits a line

On slides 6 and 7, the residual of a transaction is its observed price minus the price on the line,
$e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$. The least-squares line has the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of
the squared residuals, $\sum e_i^2$. The chart shows 15 randomly selected transactions, the line
fitted to all 1,436 transactions, and a red segment for the residual of each of the 15.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
set.seed(7)
ls_demo <- condo_resale.sf |> st_drop_geometry() |> slice_sample(n = 15) |>
  mutate(fitted = predict(condo.slr, newdata = pick(everything())))
ggplot(ls_demo, aes(AREA_SQM, SELLING_PRICE)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(condo.slr)[1], slope = coef(condo.slr)[2], colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = AREA_SQM, yend = fitted), colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = "AREA_SQM", y = "SELLING_PRICE")
```

Because the residuals are squared:

- a residual twice as large counts four times as much, so
  the `r sum(condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE > 1e7)` units sold for more than 10 million dollars weigh
  heavily in the line;
- positive and negative residuals both add to the sum of squares.
:::

::: callout-note
## How to read the regression summary

Slides 9 to 13 describe the output of `summary()`.

| Output                       | What it measures                                                       | Null hypothesis                             |
|------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **R²**                        | the share of the variation in price around its mean that the model accounts for | none, it is a measure of fit       |
| **Adjusted R²**               | R² penalised for the number of variables, so that a variable explaining nothing lowers adjusted R² | none                                     |
| **F-statistic and its p-value** | whether the model as a whole accounts for more variation than expected by chance | every slope is 0, so the mean price is as good a prediction as the model |
| **t value and Pr(>\|t\|)**    | for one coefficient, the estimate divided by its standard error         | the coefficient is 0 |

$$R^2 = \frac{\text{explained sum of squares}}{\text{total sum of squares}} = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}$$

A t value beyond about ±1.96 gives p < 0.05. The degrees of freedom are $n - p - 1$, where $n$ is
the number of transactions and $p$ the number of explanatory variables (slide 12).
:::

### Correlation between the explanatory variables

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
corrplot(cor(condo_resale[, 5:23]),
         diag = FALSE,
         order = "AOE",
         tl.pos = "td",
         tl.cex = 0.5,
         method = "number",
         type = "upper")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
cor(x)                                                    # stats
corrplot(corr, diag, order, tl.pos, tl.cex, method, type) # corrplot
```

- `condo_resale[, 5:23]` keeps columns 5 to 23, the 19 explanatory variables from `AREA_SQM` to
  `LEASEHOLD_99YR`. `cor()` computes the Pearson correlation of every pair of those variables.
- `corrplot()` prints the matrix with the correlations as numbers (`method = "number"`), above the
  diagonal only (`type = "upper"`, `diag = FALSE`), with small labels on top and on the diagonal
  (`tl.pos = "td"`, `tl.cex = 0.5`).
- `order = "AOE"` reorders the variables by the angular order of the eigenvectors (Friendly, 2002),
  which places variables with similar correlations next to each other.
- In the chapter, the `corrplot()` output is called a scatterplot matrix. It is a matrix of
  correlation coefficients.

**Example** (first two rows):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_v <- c("FREEHOLD", "LEASEHOLD_99YR")
stp_cm <- cor(condo_resale[, 5:23])[stp_v, stp_v]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(FREEHOLD = condo_resale$FREEHOLD[1:2],
                    LEASEHOLD_99YR = condo_resale$LEASEHOLD_99YR[1:2]),
             "<code>condo_resale</code>: one row per transaction"),
  step_table(tibble(` ` = stp_v, FREEHOLD = fmt_n(stp_cm[, 1], 2),
                    LEASEHOLD_99YR = fmt_n(stp_cm[, 2], 2)),
             "<code>cor()</code>: one row per variable",
             cells = tibble(row = c(1, 2), col = c("LEASEHOLD_99YR", "FREEHOLD"))))
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
cm <- cor(condo_resale[, 5:23])
cm_up <- cm
cm_up[lower.tri(cm_up, diag = TRUE)] <- NA
high_pairs <- which(abs(cm_up) > 0.6, arr.ind = TRUE)
high_pairs <- tibble(a = rownames(cm_up)[high_pairs[, 1]],
                     b = colnames(cm_up)[high_pairs[, 2]],
                     r = round(cm_up[high_pairs], 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(r)))
tenure <- table(FREEHOLD = condo_resale$FREEHOLD, LEASEHOLD_99YR = condo_resale$LEASEHOLD_99YR)
```

Three pairs have an absolute correlation above 0.6:

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(high_pairs, col.names = c("Variable", "Variable", "Correlation"))
```

`FREEHOLD` and `LEASEHOLD_99YR` are correlated at `r high_pairs$r[1]` because a unit is usually one
or the other. In all, `r tenure["0", "0"]` units have 0 in both `FREEHOLD` and `LEASEHOLD_99YR`, a
combination that matches another tenure, such as a 999-year lease. In the chapter, `LEASEHOLD_99YR`
is dropped and `FREEHOLD` is kept. The pair `PROX_CHILDCARE` and `PROX_BUS_STOP`
(`r high_pairs$r[2]`) is also kept, and the variance inflation factors of section 3.2.6 are the
check on it.

### Multiple linear regression

```{r}
condo.mlr <- lm(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_HAWKER_MARKET +
    PROX_KINDERGARTEN + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH +
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS +
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
lm(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + ..., data)                     # stats
```

- With several terms joined by `+`, `lm()` estimates one coefficient for each variable, holding the
  other variables constant. The model has 18 explanatory variables, the 19 variables of the
  correlation matrix without `LEASEHOLD_99YR`.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
mlr_p <- summary(condo.mlr)$coefficients[-1, 4]
not_sig <- names(mlr_p)[mlr_p > 0.05]
```

In all, `r length(not_sig)` variables have p >
0.05: `r paste0("\x60", not_sig, "\x60", collapse = ", ")`. R²
is `r round(summary(condo.mlr)$r.squared, 3)`.

### Revised model

```{r}
condo.mlr1 <- lm(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_MRT +
    PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA +
    PROX_PARK + PROX_PRIMARY_SCH +
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The formula is the one above without the four variables with p > 0.05. The chapter removes all
  four in one step.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
step_model <- condo.mlr
step_log <- character()
repeat {
  p <- summary(step_model)$coefficients[-1, 4]
  if (max(p) <= 0.05) break
  step_log <- c(step_log, names(which.max(p)))
  step_model <- update(step_model, as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", names(which.max(p)))))
}
same_set <- setequal(attr(terms(step_model), "term.labels"), attr(terms(condo.mlr1), "term.labels"))
```

All 14 remaining variables have p < 0.05. R² is `r round(summary(condo.mlr1)$r.squared, 4)`,
against `r round(summary(condo.mlr)$r.squared, 4)` for the full model. When several variables are
removed at once, a variable can be dropped whose p-value would fall below 0.05 once the others had
gone, because each p-value depends on the other variables in the model. Removing the variables one
at a time, the least significant first,
leaves `r ifelse(same_set, "the same 14 variables", "a different set of variables")`. The order of
removal is `r paste0("\x60", step_log, "\x60", collapse = ", ")`.

Holding the other variables constant, the coefficients of `condo.mlr1` read:

- each square metre adds `r scales::dollar(round(coef(condo.mlr1)["AREA_SQM"]))`;
- each year of age subtracts `r scales::dollar(round(-coef(condo.mlr1)["AGE"]))`;
- each kilometre further from the CBD
  subtracts `r scales::dollar(round(-coef(condo.mlr1)["PROX_CBD"]))`;
- each kilometre further from an MRT station
  subtracts `r scales::dollar(round(-coef(condo.mlr1)["PROX_MRT"]))`;
- freehold tenure adds `r scales::dollar(round(coef(condo.mlr1)["FREEHOLD"]))`;
- distance to a park, an elderly care centre, a primary school or a bus stop has a positive
  coefficient: units further away have higher prices.

The global model estimates one value of each coefficient for the whole island, and section 3.3
estimates them for each location.

### Publication-quality table

```{r}
tbl_regression(condo.mlr1, intercept = TRUE) |>
  add_glance_source_note(
    label = list(sigma ~ "\U03C3"),
    include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, AIC, statistic, p.value, sigma))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
tbl_regression(x, intercept)                              # gtsummary
add_glance_source_note(x, label, include)                 # gtsummary
```

- `tbl_regression()` formats the coefficients of `condo.mlr1` with their 95% confidence intervals
  and p-values. `intercept = TRUE` keeps the intercept, which is dropped by default.
- `add_glance_source_note()` adds the model statistics under the table. `include` picks the
  statistics. `label` renames `sigma` to the Greek letter σ, the residual standard error.

**Example** (row `AREA_SQM` and the note under the table):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_tbl <- tbl_regression(condo.mlr1, intercept = TRUE) |>
  add_glance_source_note(label = list(sigma ~ "\U03C3"),
                         include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, AIC, statistic, p.value, sigma))
stp_row <- as_tibble(stp_tbl)[2, ]
names(stp_row) <- gsub("\\*", "", names(stp_row))
stp_cf <- summary(condo.mlr1)$coefficients["AREA_SQM", ]
stp_col <- tibble(` ` = c("value", "", "means", "from"),
                  Characteristic = c(stp_row$Characteristic, "↓", "the variable", ""),
                  Beta = c(stp_row$Beta, "↓", "price change per extra m²", "coefficient of lm()"),
                  `95% CI` = c(stp_row$`95% CI`, "↓", "range for Beta, 95% confidence",
                               sprintf("Beta ± 1.96 × SE, SE = %s", fmt_n(stp_cf[["Std. Error"]]))),
                  `p-value` = c(stp_row$`p-value`, "↓", "test of Beta = 0",
                                sprintf("t = Beta / SE = %s", fmt_n(stp_cf[["t value"]], 1))))
stp_gl <- str_split_1(stp_tbl$table_styling$source_note$source_note, "; ") |> str_split_fixed(" = ", 2)
show_steps(
  step_table(stp_col, "Columns of the table",
             cells = tibble(row = 3, col = names(stp_col)[-1]), left = names(stp_col)))
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(Statistic = stp_gl[, 1], value = stp_gl[, 2],
                    means = c("share of the variation in price explained by the model",
                              "R² with a penalty for each extra variable",
                              "fit with a penalty for each coefficient; lower is better",
                              "F test of all 14 Betas = 0",
                              "p-value of the F test",
                              "residual standard error: spread of the residuals, in $")),
             "Note under the table", changed = "means", left = "means"))
```

The `(Intercept)` row is the fitted price when every variable is 0. A p-value below 0.05 means the
variable's Beta is significantly different from 0 at the 5% level.
:::

The chapter's output has the table twice, without and with the source note. Only the table with the
source note is kept here.

### Multicollinearity

```{r}
mlr.vif <- check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)
mlr.vif
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot(mlr.vif)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
check_collinearity(x)                                     # performance
plot(x)                                                   # see
```

- `check_collinearity()` computes the variance inflation factor (VIF) of each variable, with a 95%
  interval. It groups the variables as low (VIF < 5), moderate (5 to 10) or high (> 10).
- `plot()` draws the VIFs as points against those bands.
:::

All the VIFs are below 5, the largest `r round(max(mlr.vif$VIF), 2)` for `PROX_CHILDCARE`, which is
under a third of the threshold of 10 that the chapter uses.

::: callout-note
## What the variance inflation factor measures

Whether some explanatory variables are redundant (slide 14) is examined with the variance inflation
factor. The VIF of a variable is computed by regressing that variable on all the other explanatory
variables:

$$\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}$$

where $R_j^2$ is the R² of that regression.

| $R_j^2$  | VIF  | Meaning                                                                                |
|----------|------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0        | 1    | the variable is unrelated to the other variables                                                |
| 0.69     | 3.3  | `PROX_CHILDCARE`: 69% of its variation is shared with the other 13 variables            |
| 0.9      | 10   | the usual threshold: the variance of the coefficient is ten times its variance without the other variables |

The standard error of the coefficient is proportional to the square root of the VIF. A VIF of 3.3
multiplies the standard error by about 1.8, compared with a variable that shares no variation with
the other variables.
:::

### Linearity

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
check_model(condo.mlr1, check = "linearity")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
ols_plot_resid_fit(condo.mlr1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
check_model(x, check = "linearity")                       # performance
ols_plot_resid_fit(model)                                 # olsrr
```

- `check_model(check = "linearity")` plots each residual against its fitted value, with a smoothed
  line through the points. The chapter's text names `ols_plot_resid_fit()` of `olsrr`. The chapter's
  code runs `check_model()`. The plots from `ols_plot_resid_fit()` and from `check_model()` are
  drawn here. They show the same points.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
resid_bands <- tibble(fitted = fitted(condo.mlr1), resid = residuals(condo.mlr1)) |>
  mutate(band = cut(fitted, c(-Inf, 1e6, 2e6, 3e6, 4e6, Inf),
                    labels = c("below 1M", "1M to 2M", "2M to 3M", "3M to 4M", "above 4M"))) |>
  group_by(band) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(resid), sd = sd(resid))
rb <- \(b, col) scales::dollar(round(resid_bands[[col]][resid_bands$band == b], -3))
```

In the chapter, the plot of residuals against fitted values is read as showing that "most of the
data points are scattered around the 0 line". On this basis, the relationships between price and
each variable are judged linear. Grouped by band of fitted price, the residuals differ in mean and
in spread:

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(resid_bands, digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Fitted price", "Transactions", "Mean residual", "SD of residuals"))
```

- **Mean residual by fitted price.** It is `r rb("below 1M", "mean")` below a fitted price of 1
  million dollars, `r rb("2M to 3M", "mean")` between 2 and 3 million,
  and `r rb("above 4M", "mean")` above 4 million. The model underpredicts units with fitted prices
  below 1 million and above 4 million dollars, and overpredicts units between 2 and 3 million
  dollars. The pattern is the U-shape of slide 17, a sign of a nonlinear relationship in dollars.
- **Residual spread by fitted price.** The standard deviation of the residuals rises
  from `r rb("below 1M", "sd")` below 1 million dollars to `r rb("above 4M", "sd")` above 4 million
  dollars. The residuals have the funnel shape of slide 17, which is heteroscedasticity.

In section 4.1, the spread is tested, and the mean residual and the spread are examined on the log
scale.

::: callout-note
## The assumptions of linear regression

Slide 15 lists the assumptions of linear regression. The t tests and the F test of `summary()` are
valid only when all four assumptions hold.

| Assumption                       | What it requires                                                      | How it is checked on this page                      |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Linearity**                    | the price changes by a fixed amount for each unit of each variable     | residuals against fitted values (section 3.2.7)      |
| **Normality**                    | the residuals follow a normal distribution                             | Q-Q plot and Shapiro-Wilk test (section 3.2.8)       |
| **Homoscedasticity**             | the residuals have the same variance at every fitted value             | Breusch-Pagan test (section 4.1)                     |
| **Independence**                 | the residuals are uncorrelated, and for spatial data show no clustering in space | Moran's I of the residuals (section 3.2.9)         |

Residual patterns from slide 17, drawn with simulated data:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
set.seed(3)
x_sim <- runif(200, 0, 10)
patterns <- bind_rows(
  tibble(pattern = "1. random: assumptions met", fitted = x_sim, resid = rnorm(200)),
  tibble(pattern = "2. U-shape: relationship not linear", fitted = x_sim,
         resid = 0.25 * (x_sim - 5)^2 - 2 + rnorm(200, sd = 0.6)),
  tibble(pattern = "3. funnel: variance not constant", fitted = x_sim,
         resid = rnorm(200, sd = 0.15 + 0.3 * x_sim)))
ggplot(patterns, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ pattern, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "fitted value", y = "residual")
```

The residual plot of `condo.mlr1` in section 3.2.7 shows the U-shape and the funnel.
:::

### Normality of the residuals

```{r}
check_normality(condo.mlr1)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot(check_normality(condo.mlr1), type = "qq")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
check_model(condo.mlr1, check = "normality")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
check_normality(x)                                        # performance
check_model(x, check = "normality")                       # performance
```

- `check_normality()` runs the Shapiro-Wilk test on the standardised residuals. It prints whether
  the null hypothesis of normality is rejected.
- `plot(type = "qq")` draws a detrended Q-Q plot. For each residual, $x$ is the quantile of a normal
  distribution at the same rank, and $y$ is the residual minus that quantile. Residuals from a normal
  distribution give $y$ close to 0, on the line.
- `check_model(check = "normality")` draws the density of the residuals against a normal curve.

**Example**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_res <- sort(rstudent(condo.mlr1))
stp_sd <- sd(stp_res) * sqrt((length(stp_res) - 1) / length(stp_res))
stp_q <- qnorm(ppoints(length(stp_res))) * stp_sd
stp_i <- c(1, length(stp_res) %/% 2, length(stp_res))
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(rank = c("smallest", "middle", "largest"),
                    residual = fmt_n(stp_res[stp_i], 2),
                    `x: normal quantile` = fmt_n(stp_q[stp_i], 2),
                    `y: residual − x` = fmt_n(stp_res[stp_i] - stp_q[stp_i], 2)),
             "Three of the 1,436 dots of the Q-Q plot",
             added = c("x: normal quantile", "y: residual − x")))
```
:::

::: callout-note
## How to read the Q-Q plot

The shapes of a detrended Q-Q plot, drawn with simulated data:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
set.seed(4)
qq_shape <- function(z, shape) {
  z <- sort((z - mean(z)) / sd(z))
  q <- qnorm(ppoints(length(z)))
  tibble(shape = shape, x = q, y = z - q)
}
qq_shapes <- bind_rows(qq_shape(rnorm(500), "1. normal: dots on the line"),
                       qq_shape(rt(500, df = 3), "2. heavy tails: the ends move apart"),
                       qq_shape(rexp(500), "3. right skew: both ends rise"))
ggplot(qq_shapes, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ shape, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "normal quantile", y = "residual − normal quantile")
```

- **Left end below the line**: the smallest residuals are more negative than in a normal
  distribution.
- **Left end above the line**: the smallest residuals are closer to 0 than in a normal distribution,
  as in panel 3.
- **Right end above the line**: the largest residuals are more positive than in a normal
  distribution.
- **A wave in the middle**: most residuals are closer to 0 than in a normal distribution.

In the Q-Q plot of `condo.mlr1`, the right end rises to `r round(max(stp_res - stp_q))`, the left
end is slightly below the line, and the middle has a wave. The residuals have heavy tails, mostly on
the right: a few units sold for far more than the model predicts.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
res_mlr <- residuals(condo.mlr1)
kurt <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^4) / sd(x)^4
```

The test rejects normality (p < 0.001). In the chapter, the rejection is reported. The residuals are
then described, from the density plot, as resembling a "normal distribution". The plots above show
departures from a normal distribution:

- in the Q-Q plot, the largest standardised residual is `r round(max(rstandard(condo.mlr1)), 1)`,
  where the largest of 1,436 normal values would be about `r round(qnorm(1 - 0.5 / 1436), 1)`;
- in the density plot, the right tail extends beyond 10 million dollars;
- the skewness of the residuals is `r round(skew(res_mlr), 2)`, against 0 for a normal distribution;
- the kurtosis of the residuals is `r round(kurt(res_mlr), 1)`, against 3 for a normal distribution.

The chapter's note quotes the `performance` help page: with large samples, the test is almost always
significant, so a visual check is advised. Here the visual check gives the same result as the test.
The departure may reflect the right tail of the prices seen in section 3.1.1.

### Spatial autocorrelation of the residuals

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf |>
  mutate(MLR_RES = residuals(condo.mlr1))
```

```{r}
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "MLR_RES",
          size = 0.3,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            n = 10, style = "quantile",
            values = "-brewer.rd_bu", midpoint = 0),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residual")) +
  tm_title("OLS residuals, quantile classes") +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses four functions:

```r
mutate(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
tm_dots(fill, size, fill.scale, fill.legend)              # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(n, style, values, midpoint)            # tmap
tm_title(text)                                            # tmap
```

- `mutate()` adds the residual of each transaction as `MLR_RES`. In the chapter, the residuals are
  first copied into the data frame `mlr.output`, which no later step reads. The residuals are then
  joined with `cbind()` under a new column name. The chapter's method and `mutate()` produce the
  same column.
- `tm_scale_intervals(n = 10, style = "quantile")` divides the residuals into ten classes of equal
  size. `values = "-brewer.rd_bu"` is the red-blue palette reversed, so that negative residuals are
  blue and positive residuals are red. `midpoint = 0` centres the palette on zero.
- In the chapter, this map is coded for view mode with `#| eval: false`, so the chapter's page shows
  no map. The map is drawn here as a static map.

**Example** (first two rows):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_p <- condo_resale.sf$SELLING_PRICE[1:2]
stp_f <- fitted(condo.mlr1)[1:2]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(SELLING_PRICE = fmt_n(stp_p),
                    MLR_RES = sprintf("%s &minus; %s = %s", fmt_n(stp_p), fmt_n(stp_f),
                                      fmt_n(stp_p - stp_f)) |> lapply(htmltools::HTML)),
             "<code>MLR_RES</code> = price &minus; fitted price", added = "MLR_RES"))
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
res_pa <- st_join(condo_resale.sf, mpsz_svy21[, "PLN_AREA_N"]) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_res = mean(MLR_RES)) |>
  filter(n >= 20) |>
  arrange(mean_res)
rp <- \(a) scales::dollar(round(res_pa$mean_res[res_pa$PLN_AREA_N == a], -3))
```

Red points are units that sold for more than the model predicts. Blue points are units that sold for
less. Among the `r nrow(res_pa)` planning areas with at least 20 transactions, the mean residual is
highest in Newton (`r rp("NEWTON")`), River Valley (`r rp("RIVER VALLEY")`) and Jurong West
(`r rp("JURONG WEST")`). The mean residual is lowest in Queenstown (`r rp("QUEENSTOWN")`), Bishan
(`r rp("BISHAN")`) and Kallang (`r rp("KALLANG")`). Newton and River Valley, and Queenstown, Bishan
and Kallang, are all in the Central Region, so the mean residual changes sign over short distances
inside it. On slide 27, the question is why the spatial distribution of the residuals should be
examined. A residual is the difference between the observed price and the price predicted from the
explanatory variables. If neighbouring residuals are alike, a factor that varies with location and
is absent from the model may affect the price.

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf |>
  mutate(nb = st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry), upper = 1500),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)
```

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES,
                  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                  alternative = "two.sided",
                  nsim = 499)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
st_dist_band(geometry, lower = 0, upper)                  # sfdep
st_weights(nb, style = "W")                               # sfdep
global_moran_perm(x, nb, wt, alternative, nsim)           # sfdep
```

- `st_dist_band(upper = 1500)` makes every transaction within 1,500 m a neighbour. The distances are
  in metres because the points are in SVY21.
- `st_weights(style = "W")` row-standardises the weights, so that each transaction's neighbours have
  weights summing to 1.
- `global_moran_perm()` computes Moran's I of the residuals. It compares that value with 499 values
  from random permutations of the residuals over the points.

**Example** (first two rows):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_nb <- condo_resale.sf$nb[1:2]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(nb = sapply(stp_nb, \(x) sprintf("%d rows: %s, ...", length(x),
                                                     paste(head(x, 3), collapse = ", "))),
                    wt = sapply(stp_nb, \(x) sprintf("1/%d = %s each", length(x),
                                                     fmt_n(1 / length(x), 4)))),
             "<code>mutate(nb = ..., wt = ...)</code>", added = c("nb", "wt")))
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
nb_card <- lengths(condo_resale.sf$nb)
nb_comp <- n.comp.nb(condo_resale.sf$nb)$nc
```

Moran's I of the OLS residuals is 0.144, above its expected value of about 0 under randomness. The
residuals are positively autocorrelated (one-sided permutation p = 0.002, section 4.2): units within
1.5 km of each other tend to have similar residuals. Each transaction has between `r min(nb_card)`
and `r max(nb_card)` neighbours within 1.5 km, with a median of `r median(nb_card)`. The neighbour
graph has `r nb_comp` separate components.

The printed p-value, "< 2.2e-16", is an error. With 499 permutations, the smallest one-sided p-value
of a permutation test is 1/500 = 0.002, which occurs when the observed I exceeds all 499 simulated
values. `sfdep` returns exactly 0 for the two-sided test, which R prints as "< 2.2e-16". The chapter
reports "< 2.2e-16" as the p-value. The conclusion is the same as the chapter's, because 0.002 is
one twenty-fifth of 0.05.

::: callout-note
## Why autocorrelated residuals matter

On slides 24 to 26, spatial non-stationarity is defined as the same stimulus provoking a different
response in different parts of the study region. A single global model assumes that each square
metre and each kilometre from the CBD is worth the same everywhere in Singapore.

Slide 25 lists the reasons for a relationship to vary over space:

| Reason                                     | What it is                                                      | Remedy                                      |
|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| sampling variation                         | local estimates differ by chance; the relationship is the same   | a significance test of the local variation   |
| intrinsic differences in relationships      | real non-stationarity: buyers value features differently by area | a local model, such as GWR                 |
| model misspecification                     | a missing variable that varies over space                        | addition of the variable                    |

Autocorrelated residuals occur with intrinsic differences in relationships and with model
misspecification. The OLS standard errors are computed on the assumption of independent residuals,
so with positive autocorrelation the standard errors are too small and the t values of section 3.2.4
are too large. Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1996) developed GWR to explore relationships
that differ intrinsically between places.
:::

## Geographically weighted regression

::: callout-note
## How GWR estimates a local model

GWR fits one regression at every transaction. The formula of slide 30 has the same terms as OLS, but
each coefficient depends on the location $(u_i, v_i)$ of transaction $i$:

$$y_i = \beta_0(u_i, v_i) + \sum_k \beta_k(u_i, v_i)\, x_{ik} + \varepsilon_i$$

With a Gaussian kernel, each local regression uses all 1,436 transactions, weighted by their
distance from transaction $i$ (slide 31). The weight is 1 at distance 0 and 0.61 at a distance equal
to the bandwidth. The weights are computed by a kernel function of the distance $d_{ij}$ and the
bandwidth $b$ (slide 32). The kernels used on this page:

| Kernel     | Weight                                                                 | Beyond the bandwidth        |
|------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Gaussian   | $w_{ij} = \exp\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(d_{ij}/b)^2\right)$                  | positive; 0.14 at twice the bandwidth |
| Bisquare   | $w_{ij} = \left(1 - (d_{ij}/b)^2\right)^2$ if $d_{ij} < b$, otherwise 0 | zero                       |

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3
tibble(d = seq(0, 3000, 10)) |>
  mutate(Gaussian = exp(-0.5 * (d / 1000)^2),
         Bisquare = ifelse(d < 1000, (1 - (d / 1000)^2)^2, 0)) |>
  pivot_longer(-d, names_to = "kernel", values_to = "w") |>
  ggplot(aes(d, w, colour = kernel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1000, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("firebrick", "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "distance from the regression point (m)", y = "weight", colour = NULL,
       title = "Kernel weights, b = 1,000 m")
```

The bandwidth is fixed or adaptive (slide 34):

- **fixed**: the same distance $b$ everywhere, in metres. The number of transactions within $b$ is
  larger where transactions are dense.
- **adaptive**: $b$ at each point is the distance to its $k$-th nearest transaction, so every local
  regression has $k$ transactions within the bandwidth. `bw.gwr()` returns $k$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
xy <- st_coordinates(condo_resale.sf)
dmat <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
n_near <- rowSums(dmat <= 971.3405) - 1
pa_region <- st_join(condo_resale.sf, mpsz_svy21[, c("PLN_AREA_N", "REGION_N")])
north_idx <- which(pa_region$REGION_N == "NORTH REGION")
pick_pt <- c(which.max(n_near), north_idx[which.min(n_near[north_idx])])
pick_area <- stringr::str_to_title(pa_region$PLN_AREA_N[pick_pt])
n_within <- sapply(pick_pt, \(i) sum(dmat[i, ] <= 971.3405) - 1)
b_ad_north <- sort(dmat[pick_pt[2], ])[31]
```

Kernel weights for the transactions in `r pick_area[1]` (the most other transactions within 971 m,
of all 1,436) and in `r pick_area[2]` (the fewest, in the North Region), under the fixed and the
adaptive bandwidth chosen in sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.3:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
weights_demo <- map_dfr(seq_along(pick_pt), \(k) {
  i <- pick_pt[k]
  d <- dmat[i, ]
  b_ad <- sort(d)[31]
  bind_rows(
    tibble(scheme = "fixed, b = 971 m", x = xy[, 1], y = xy[, 2], w = exp(-0.5 * (d / 971.3405)^2)),
    tibble(scheme = "adaptive, k = 30", x = xy[, 1], y = xy[, 2], w = exp(-0.5 * (d / b_ad)^2))) |>
    mutate(point = paste0(c("dense: ", "sparse: "), pick_area)[k])
})
ggplot(weights_demo, aes(x, y, colour = w)) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(mpsz_svy21), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = tidyr::crossing(
               tibble(point = paste0(c("dense: ", "sparse: "), pick_area),
                      x = xy[pick_pt, 1], y = xy[pick_pt, 2]),
               scheme = c("fixed, b = 971 m", "adaptive, k = 30")),
             aes(x, y), colour = "black", shape = 4, size = 3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  facet_grid(point ~ scheme) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "weight")
```

The cross marks the regression point. With the fixed bandwidth of 971 m, the number of other
transactions within 971 m is `r n_within[1]` in `r pick_area[1]` and `r n_within[2]`
in `r pick_area[2]`. With the adaptive bandwidth, the bandwidth at the transaction
in `r pick_area[2]` is `r round(b_ad_north)` m, the distance to its 30th nearest transaction. At the
transaction in `r pick_area[1]`, the bandwidth is `r round(sort(dmat[pick_pt[1], ])[31])` m.
:::

::: callout-note
## How the bandwidth is chosen

Slide 35 lists the criteria for the bandwidth. `bw.gwr()` searches for the bandwidth that minimises
the selected criterion.

- **Cross-validation (CV)**: $CV = \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_{\neq i})^2$, where $\hat{y}_{\neq i}$ is
  the prediction for transaction $i$ from a local regression that leaves $i$ out. A bandwidth near 0
  reproduces the neighbours of each point but predicts the left-out point poorly. A bandwidth that
  covers all transactions gives the global model.
- **AICc**: the corrected Akaike information criterion, which adds a penalty for the effective
  number of parameters of the model to its fit. The formula on slide 35 is labelled AIC. Its last
  term, $n\{(n + \mathrm{tr}(S))/(n - 2 - \mathrm{tr}(S))\}$, makes it the corrected form, AICc.

Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1996, section 3) introduced the CV score for GWR. They
minimised it by golden-section search, the search that `bw.gwr()` uses. CV is used in sections 3.3.1
and 3.3.3, as in the chapter.
:::

### Fixed bandwidth

```{r}
#| results: hide
bw.fixed <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY +
    FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = FALSE,
  longlat = FALSE)
```

```{r}
bw.fixed
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
bw.gwr(formula, data, approach, kernel, adaptive, longlat) # GWmodel
```

- `bw.gwr()` evaluates a series of bandwidths by golden-section search. It returns the bandwidth
  with the lowest score. Each bandwidth evaluated is printed. The chunk option `results: hide` keeps
  the 20 lines of the search off the page.
- `approach = "CV"` scores each bandwidth by cross-validation. `kernel = "gaussian"` gives the
  Gaussian weights of slide 32. `adaptive = FALSE` makes the bandwidth a distance.
- `longlat = FALSE` computes Euclidean distances on the projected coordinates.

**Example**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_d <- sort(as.numeric(st_distance(condo_resale.sf[1, ], condo_resale.sf)))[c(1, 2, 30)]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(`distance d (m)` = fmt_n(stp_d),
                    weight = sprintf("exp(&minus;0.5 &times; (%s / %s)²) = %s", fmt_n(stp_d),
                                     fmt_n(bw.fixed), fmt_n(exp(-0.5 * (stp_d / bw.fixed)^2), 2)) |>
                      lapply(htmltools::HTML)),
             "Row 1 and two of its neighbours, Gaussian kernel, fixed b", added = "weight"))
```
:::

The chosen bandwidth is `r round(bw.fixed, 1)` m. The chapter has a quiz on why the bandwidth is in
metres. The bandwidth is in metres because the points are in SVY21 (EPSG:3414), whose unit is the
metre. With `longlat = FALSE`, the distances are measured in that unit. If the same points were in
WGS 84 degrees and `longlat = TRUE` were set, `GWmodel` would compute great-circle distances in
kilometres.

### GWR with the fixed bandwidth

```{r}
gwr.fixed <- gwr.basic(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY +
    FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  bw = bw.fixed,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  longlat = FALSE)
gwr.fixed
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
gwr.basic(formula, data, bw, kernel, adaptive = FALSE, longlat) # GWmodel
```

- `gwr.basic()` fits a weighted regression at each of the 1,436 points, using the bandwidth and
  kernel supplied as arguments. It returns a list of class `gwrm`. Printing the list gives the
  report of slide 36.
:::

::: callout-note
## How to read the report of `gwr.basic()`

The report has the parts listed on slide 36:

| Part                                    | Contents                                                                        |
|-----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Package model**                        | the call, the response and the explanatory variables                            |
| **Results of global regression**         | the OLS model of section 3.2.4, with its AIC, AICc and BIC                       |
| **Results of GWR**                       | the kernel and bandwidth, a five-number summary of each local coefficient, and the diagnostics |
| **SDF**                                  | the local results, one row per transaction, in `gwr.fixed$SDF` (section 3.3.5)   |

The diagnostics, in the order printed:

- **Effective number of parameters**: the total number of parameters of the local fits. OLS uses 15
  coefficients. With a small bandwidth, each point has its own coefficients, and the number rises
  towards $n$.
- **AICc**: computed on the same response as the AICc of the global regression in the same report,
  so the AICc values are comparable. A smaller AICc indicates a better fit after the penalty for the
  effective number of parameters.
- **R² and adjusted R²**: computed from the fitted values of the local regressions.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
ols_aicc <- gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$AICc
diag_tbl <- function(g) c(AICc = g$GW.diagnostic$AICc, R2 = g$GW.diagnostic$gw.R2,
                          adjR2 = g$GW.diagnostic$gwR2.adj, enp = g$GW.diagnostic$enp)
fx <- diag_tbl(gwr.fixed)
lm_aicc <- AIC(condo.mlr1) + 2 * 16 * 17 / (1436 - 16 - 1)
```

The AICc of the GWR is `r format(round(fx["AICc"], 2), nsmall = 2)`,
against `r format(round(lm_aicc, 2), nsmall = 2)` for the global model. R² rose
from `r round(summary(condo.mlr1)$r.squared, 3)` to `r round(fx["R2"], 3)`. The local fits
have `r round(fx["enp"])` effective parameters, against 15 for OLS. In the chapter, the AICc is
called "significantly smaller". AICc is a measure of fit with a penalty for complexity, with no
significance level attached. The difference is tested in section 4.6.

### Adaptive bandwidth

```{r}
#| results: hide
bw.adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS +
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
```

```{r}
bw.adaptive
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The call of section 3.3.1 is used with `adaptive = TRUE`, so the bandwidth returned is a number of
  nearest neighbours.

**Example**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_b30 <- sort(as.numeric(st_distance(condo_resale.sf[1, ], condo_resale.sf)))[bw.adaptive]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(`distance d (m)` = fmt_n(stp_d),
                    weight = sprintf("exp(&minus;0.5 &times; (%s / %s)²) = %s", fmt_n(stp_d),
                                     fmt_n(stp_b30), fmt_n(exp(-0.5 * (stp_d / stp_b30)^2), 2)) |>
                      lapply(htmltools::HTML)),
             sprintf(paste("Same rows as above; for row 1, b = distance to its %dth nearest",
                           "(itself included) = %s m"), bw.adaptive, fmt_n(stp_b30)),
             added = "weight"))
```
:::

The chosen bandwidth is `r bw.adaptive` nearest neighbours.

### GWR with the adaptive bandwidth

```{r}
gwr.adaptive <- gwr.basic(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  bw = bw.adaptive,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
gwr.adaptive
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The call of section 3.3.2 is used with `bw = bw.adaptive` and `adaptive = TRUE`.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
ad <- diag_tbl(gwr.adaptive)
coef_range <- function(g, v) range(g$SDF[[v]])
```

The AICc of the adaptive model is `r format(round(ad["AICc"], 2), nsmall = 2)`, lower than the AICc
of the fixed model, `r format(round(fx["AICc"], 2), nsmall = 2)`. The adaptive model has an R²
of `r round(ad["R2"], 3)` and `r round(ad["enp"])` effective parameters.

```{r}
#| echo: false
diag_compare <- tibble(
  Model = c("OLS, `condo.mlr1`", "GWR, fixed bandwidth", "GWR, adaptive bandwidth"),
  Bandwidth = c("n/a", paste(round(bw.fixed), "m"), paste(bw.adaptive, "neighbours")),
  AICc = c(lm_aicc, fx["AICc"], ad["AICc"]),
  `R²` = c(summary(condo.mlr1)$r.squared, fx["R2"], ad["R2"]),
  `Adjusted R²` = c(summary(condo.mlr1)$adj.r.squared, fx["adjR2"], ad["adjR2"]),
  `Effective parameters` = c(15, fx["enp"], ad["enp"]))
kable(diag_compare, digits = c(0, 0, 1, 3, 3, 0), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The AICc of the fixed and of the adaptive GWR model is lower than the AICc of OLS
by `r format(round(lm_aicc - fx["AICc"]), big.mark = ",")`
and `r format(round(lm_aicc - ad["AICc"]), big.mark = ",")`. The five-number summaries in the report
show implausible local coefficients. In the adaptive model, the local intercept ranges
from `r scales::dollar(coef_range(gwr.adaptive, "Intercept")[1])`
to `r scales::dollar(coef_range(gwr.adaptive, "Intercept")[2])`, and the coefficient of `PROX_MRT`
ranges from `r scales::dollar(coef_range(gwr.adaptive, "PROX_MRT")[1])`
to `r scales::dollar(coef_range(gwr.adaptive, "PROX_MRT")[2])` per kilometre.

### Contents of the GWR output

```{r}
condo_resale.sf.adaptive <- gwr.adaptive$SDF
class(condo_resale.sf.adaptive)
st_crs(condo_resale.sf.adaptive)$epsg
names(condo_resale.sf.adaptive)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `gwr.adaptive$SDF` holds the local results. In the chapter, it is converted with `st_as_sf()` and
  `st_transform(crs = 3414)`. Since the input was an sf object, `GWmodel` 2.4 returns an sf object
  in EPSG:3414, so `st_as_sf()` and `st_transform(crs = 3414)` change nothing and are left out.

**Example** (first two rows):

```{r}
#| echo: false
stp_g <- gwr.adaptive$SDF[1:2, ]
show_steps(
  step_table(tibble(AREA_SQM = paste(condo_resale.sf$AREA_SQM[1:2], "m²")),
             "<code>condo_resale.sf</code>: floor area", changed = "AREA_SQM"),
  step_table(tibble(AREA_SQM = paste0("$", fmt_n(stp_g$AREA_SQM), " per m²"),
                    AREA_SQM_SE = fmt_n(stp_g$AREA_SQM_SE),
                    AREA_SQM_TV = sprintf("%s / %s = %s", fmt_n(stp_g$AREA_SQM),
                                          fmt_n(stp_g$AREA_SQM_SE), fmt_n(stp_g$AREA_SQM_TV, 2))),
             "<code>gwr.adaptive$SDF</code>: local coefficient", changed = "AREA_SQM",
             added = c("AREA_SQM_SE", "AREA_SQM_TV")))
```
:::

| Columns                          | Contents                                                                         |
|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Intercept`, `AREA_SQM`, ...      | the 15 local coefficients                                                        |
| `y`, `yhat`, `residual`           | observed price, fitted price, and their difference                               |
| `CV_Score`, `Stud_residual`       | the leave-one-out residual, and the studentised residual                         |
| `..._SE`                          | the standard error of each local coefficient                                     |
| `..._TV`                          | the local t-value, coefficient divided by standard error                         |
| `Local_R2`                        | the R² of each local regression                                                  |

The chapter's list of outputs in section 13.9.3 is taken from the help of the GWR tool in ArcGIS. In
the `GWmodel` output, the condition number and the standardised residuals of that list are absent:

- **condition number**: there is no column for the condition number. `GWmodel` computes local
  condition numbers with a separate function, `gwr.collin.diagno()`, which is applied in section
  4.4;
- **standardised residuals**: the output has studentised residuals, `Stud_residual`.

In the chapter, the object is also called a SpatialPointsDataFrame. With sf input, it is an sf data
frame.

```{r}
summary(gwr.adaptive$SDF$yhat)
```

The fitted prices of the adaptive model range
from `r scales::dollar(round(min(gwr.adaptive$SDF$yhat)))`
to `r scales::dollar(round(max(gwr.adaptive$SDF$yhat)))`.

### Local R²

```{r}
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +
  tm_dots(fill = "Local_R2",
          size = 0.3,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local R²")) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The chapter's chunk uses the arguments of `tmap` version 3 (`col`, `border.col`,
  `set.zoom.limits`) and is set to `eval: false`, so the chapter's page has no map. The map above
  uses the version 4 arguments, `fill`, `fill.scale` and `fill.legend`. It is drawn in plot mode.
- `style = "pretty"` gives classes with round break values, such as 0.6, 0.7 and 0.8.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
lr2 <- gwr.adaptive$SDF$Local_R2
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lr2_pa <- st_join(condo_resale.sf.adaptive, mpsz_svy21[, c("PLN_AREA_N", "REGION_N")]) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N) |>
  summarise(n = n(), r2 = median(Local_R2)) |>
  filter(n >= 15)
lp <- \(a) round(lr2_pa$r2[lr2_pa$PLN_AREA_N == a], 2)
```

Local R² ranges from `r round(min(lr2), 2)` to `r round(max(lr2), 2)`, with a median
of `r round(median(lr2), 2)`. Among planning areas with at least 15 transactions, a minimum that
avoids medians of very few values, the median local R² is lowest in Bishan (`r lp("BISHAN")`), Toa
Payoh (`r lp("TOA PAYOH")`) and Bukit Merah (`r lp("BUKIT MERAH")`), in the Central Region. The
median local R² is highest in Woodlands (`r lp("WOODLANDS")`), Choa Chu Kang
(`r lp("CHOA CHU KANG")`) and Yishun (`r lp("YISHUN")`), in the north and west.

::: callout-note
## How to read local R²

Local R² is the R² of one local regression: the share of the weighted variation in price near that
transaction that its local coefficients account for.

- **High value.** A high value means the local model fits the prices of the nearby units well.
- **Low value.** A low value may reflect a local factor that the variables do not capture, such as a
  view, a developer's brand or a prestige address. The chapter makes the same point about missing
  variables.
- **Spatial dependence.** Neighbouring regressions share most of their data, so a smooth map is
  expected.
- **Comparison with the global R².** The local R² uses weighted data and the global R² unweighted
  data, so their values are on different bases.
:::
