```{r}
#| echo: false
area_tv_v <- gwr.adaptive$SDF$AREA_SQM_TV
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
se_region <- st_join(condo_resale.sf.adaptive, mpsz_svy21[, "REGION_N"]) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(REGION_N) |>
  summarise(se = median(AREA_SQM_SE))
sr <- \(r) scales::dollar(round(se_region$se[se_region$REGION_N == r]))
```

The standard error of the floor-area coefficient is smallest in the Central Region
(median `r sr("CENTRAL REGION")` per m²) and largest in the North Region (`r sr("NORTH REGION")`).
Floor area varies more in the Central Region, with a standard deviation
of `r round(sd(condo_pa$AREA_SQM[condo_pa$REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION"]))` m²
against `r round(sd(condo_pa$AREA_SQM[condo_pa$REGION_N == "NORTH REGION"]))` m² in the North
Region. A wider spread of the variable gives a more precise slope. The t-value is above 1.96
at `r sum(area_tv_v > 1.96)` of the 1,436 transactions, and below −1.96 at 0 transactions, so the
effect of floor area is positive and significant at the 5% level
at `r round(100 * mean(area_tv_v > 1.96))`% of the transactions. The coefficients themselves are
mapped with their significance in section 4.7.

# Part 2: Review and extension

Chapter 13 was reproduced in Part 1. In Part 2, the choices in the chapter's method are compared
with the Lesson 9 slides and readings. A GWR is then fitted, and its coefficients are tested and
mapped with their significance, as the readings describe.

| Section | What is done                                                                       | Source                                                                 |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|         | **Checking the chapter's method**                                                  |                                                                        |
| 4.1     | Fit the hedonic model on the log of the price and repeat the diagnostics           | slides 15 to 21; chapter 13.7.1                                        |
| 4.2     | Compute the correct p-value of Moran's I of the residuals                          | slide 28; Brunsdon et al. (1999, p. 497); chapter 13.8.6.4             |
| 4.3     | Compare kernels, fixed and adaptive bandwidths, and CV with AICc                   | slides 32 to 35; Brunsdon et al. (1996); Gollini et al. (2015, p. 19)  |
| 4.4     | Compute the local collinearity diagnostics for the most extreme local coefficients | Gollini et al. (2015), section 7; Lu et al. (2014), section 5.2        |
|         | **Completing the analysis**                                                        |                                                                        |
| 4.5     | Fit GWR on the log scale; compare OLS and GWR in dollars and in logs               | sections 4.1 to 4.4; Matthews and Yang (2012, p. 154)                  |
| 4.6     | Test whether GWR improves on OLS and which coefficients vary                       | Brunsdon et al. (1996, 1999); Lu et al. (2014), section 4.2            |
| 4.7     | Map the coefficients with their significance, adjusted for multiple tests          | Mennis (2006); Matthews and Yang (2012); Lu et al. (2014), section 5.1 |

The formula of the revised model, `condo.mlr1`, is defined below for the price in dollars and for
the price in logs:

```{r}
x_vars <- c("AREA_SQM", "AGE", "PROX_CBD", "PROX_CHILDCARE", "PROX_ELDERLYCARE",
            "PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA", "PROX_MRT", "PROX_PARK", "PROX_PRIMARY_SCH",
            "PROX_SHOPPING_MALL", "PROX_BUS_STOP", "NO_Of_UNITS",
            "FAMILY_FRIENDLY", "FREEHOLD")
f_dollar <- reformulate(x_vars, response = "SELLING_PRICE")
f_log <- reformulate(x_vars, response = "LOG_SELLING_PRICE")
condo_gw <- condo_resale.sf |> select(SELLING_PRICE, LOG_SELLING_PRICE, all_of(x_vars))
```

`reformulate()` builds the formula from the vector of names. `condo_gw` keeps only the columns used
by the models. The neighbour list and weights added in section 3.2.9 are dropped, because `GWmodel`
reads only plain data columns.

## Response scale: price in dollars and log price

In section 3.1.1, `LOG_SELLING_PRICE` was computed because the prices were skewed
(skewness `r round(skew_price, 2)`). Every model in Part 1 then used the price in dollars. In
sections 3.2.7 and 3.2.8, the residuals departed from the assumptions of slide 15: the mean residual
was U-shaped against the fitted price, the spread increased with the fitted price, and the
standardised residuals reached `r round(max(rstandard(condo.mlr1)), 1)` in the upper tail.

On slide 18, the idea that the response should be transformed because its values are large is called
a myth. On slides 19 to 21, the response is transformed because the diagnostic plot shows a
violation. After the transformation, the violation disappears. The residual plot of section 3.2.7
shows such a violation. On the log scale, a coefficient $b$ is a proportional effect: one more unit
of the variable multiplies the price by $e^b$, a change of $100(e^b - 1)$ per cent. One more
kilometre from the MRT then changes the price of a 3-million-dollar unit by more dollars than the
price of a 1-million-dollar unit. The U-shaped mean residual and the widening spread in section
3.2.7 are consistent with proportional effects of this kind.

The question for this section is whether the log scale removes the departures found in Part 1, and
how it changes the coefficients.

```{r}
condo.mlr1.log <- lm(f_log, data = condo_resale.sf)

diagnose <- function(m) {
  r <- residuals(m)
  bp <- bptest(m)
  tibble(skewness = skew(r), kurtosis = kurt(r),
         `Shapiro-Wilk W` = shapiro.test(rstandard(m))$statistic,
         `Breusch-Pagan` = bp$statistic,
         `BP p-value` = format.pval(bp$p.value, eps = 0.001))
}
bind_rows(dollars = diagnose(condo.mlr1), logs = diagnose(condo.mlr1.log), .id = "Response") |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4))
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6.5
resid_panel <- function(m, title) {
  tibble(fitted = fitted(m), resid = rstandard(m)) |>
    ggplot(aes(fitted, resid)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "firebrick") +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +
    labs(title = title, x = "fitted value", y = "standardised residual")
}
qq_panel <- function(m) {
  tibble(r = rstandard(m)) |>
    ggplot(aes(sample = r)) + stat_qq(size = 0.6) + stat_qq_line(colour = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = "normal quantile", y = "standardised residual")
}
(resid_panel(condo.mlr1, "price in dollars") | resid_panel(condo.mlr1.log, "log of the price")) /
  (qq_panel(condo.mlr1) | qq_panel(condo.mlr1.log))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
dg_d <- diagnose(condo.mlr1)
dg_l <- diagnose(condo.mlr1.log)
pct <- \(b) 100 * (exp(b) - 1)
cl <- coef(condo.mlr1.log)
p_log <- summary(condo.mlr1.log)$coefficients[-1, 4]
ns_log <- names(p_log)[p_log > 0.05]
```

On the log scale:

- **Mean of the residuals.** The smoothed line of the standardised residuals is flat up to a fitted
  log price of about 15.5, about 5 million dollars. Above a fitted log price of 15.5 the line slopes
  downward; `r sum(fitted(condo.mlr1.log) > 15.5)` units are in that range.
- **Skewness and kurtosis.** The skewness of the residuals fell from `r round(dg_d$skewness, 2)`
  to `r round(dg_l$skewness, 2)`, against 0 for a normal distribution. The kurtosis fell
  from `r round(dg_d$kurtosis, 1)` to `r round(dg_l$kurtosis, 1)`, against 3. In the Q-Q plot, the
  points lie on the line except at the lower end, where `r sum(rstandard(condo.mlr1.log) < -3)`
  units have standardised residuals below −3: they sold for much less than their fitted prices. The
  Shapiro-Wilk test still rejects normality (W = `r round(dg_l[["Shapiro-Wilk W"]], 3)`, p < 0.001).
  With 1,436 residuals, a small departure from normality is enough for the test to reject it, as
  noted on the `performance` help page quoted in section 3.2.8.
- **Variance of the residuals.** The Breusch-Pagan test rejects homoscedasticity in dollars and in
  logs (statistic `r round(dg_d[["Breusch-Pagan"]])` in dollars, `r round(dg_l[["Breusch-Pagan"]])`
  in logs, p < 0.001 for both). In logs, the spread is largest above a fitted log price of 15.

The coefficients become proportional effects:

| Variable                | Coefficient in logs                                | Effect on the price                                         |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `AREA_SQM`              | `r signif(cl["AREA_SQM"], 3)`                        | `r round(pct(cl["AREA_SQM"]), 2)`% per square metre          |
| `AGE`                   | `r signif(cl["AGE"], 3)`                             | `r round(pct(cl["AGE"]), 2)`% per year                       |
| `PROX_CBD`              | `r signif(cl["PROX_CBD"], 3)`                        | `r round(pct(cl["PROX_CBD"]), 1)`% per km                    |
| `PROX_MRT`              | `r signif(cl["PROX_MRT"], 3)`                        | `r round(pct(cl["PROX_MRT"]), 1)`% per km                    |
| `FREEHOLD`              | `r signif(cl["FREEHOLD"], 3)`                        | `r round(pct(cl["FREEHOLD"]), 1)`% for freehold tenure       |

Four variables that were significant in dollars have p > 0.05 in
logs: `r paste0("\x60", ns_log, "\x60", collapse = ", ")`. The variables with p > 0.05 in logs are
kept, so that the models in dollars and in logs have the same variables and can be compared in
section 4.5. R² is `r round(summary(condo.mlr1.log)$r.squared, 3)` in logs
and `r round(summary(condo.mlr1)$r.squared, 3)` in dollars. Each R² is a share of the variation of a
different response, the log price in one model and the price in dollars in the other, so the two R²
values measure different quantities.

## Residual autocorrelation: p-values of Moran's I

Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1999, p. 497) write that if relationships that vary over space
are modelled with a global regression, "the error terms in the global regression model will exhibit
spatial autocorrelation". In their house price example, the positive and negative OLS residuals
"exhibited strong spatial clustering" (p. 506). Moran's I of the OLS residuals is the check for
this. In section 3.2.9, the p-value of Moran's I of the residuals was printed as "< 2.2e-16", from a
permutation test with 499 simulations.

A permutation test ranks the observed statistic among the simulated statistics. With 499
simulations, the one-sided p-value is

$$p = \frac{1 + \text{number of simulated I at least as large as the observed I}}{499 + 1}$$

and its smallest possible value is 1/500 = 0.002. A p-value below 0.002 requires more than 499
simulations. The test on slide 28 is `lm.morantest()`. Its p-value comes from the normal
approximation, with the expected I of regression residuals, −0.0055 here, in place of 0. The
question for this section is the correct p-value of Moran's I, from the permutation test and from
`lm.morantest()`, for the residuals in dollars and in logs.

```{r}
lw_1500 <- nb2listw(condo_resale.sf$nb, style = "W")
set.seed(1234)
mc_dollar <- moran.mc(residuals(condo.mlr1), lw_1500, nsim = 499)
set.seed(1234)
mc_log <- moran.mc(residuals(condo.mlr1.log), lw_1500, nsim = 499)
lmt_dollar <- lm.morantest(condo.mlr1, lw_1500)
lmt_log <- lm.morantest(condo.mlr1.log, lw_1500)

tibble(Response = c("dollars", "logs"),
       `Moran's I` = c(mc_dollar$statistic, mc_log$statistic),
       `Permutation p` = c(mc_dollar$p.value, mc_log$p.value),
       `Expected I` = c(lmt_dollar$estimate[2], lmt_log$estimate[2]),
       `z (lm.morantest)` = c(lmt_dollar$statistic, lmt_log$statistic),
       `p (lm.morantest)` = format.pval(c(lmt_dollar$p.value, lmt_log$p.value), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 4, 3, 5, 1, 3))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
mc_two <- function(mc) min(1, 2 * min(mc$p.value, 1 - mc$p.value + 1 / 500))
```

The one-sided permutation p-value is `r mc_dollar$p.value` in dollars, the smallest value possible
with 499 simulations. The two-sided p-value is `r 2 * mc_dollar$p.value`. The `lm.morantest()`
z-value of `r round(lmt_dollar$statistic, 1)` corresponds to a p-value below 2.2e-16. The
permutation test and `lm.morantest()` each reject spatial randomness of the residuals, which agrees
with the conclusion of chapter 13.

On the log scale, Moran's I rose from `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_dollar$statistic)`
to `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_log$statistic)`. The log transformation reduced the skewness of the
residuals (section 4.1). The rise in I may reflect the smaller number of extreme residuals, which
inflate the denominator of I.

## Bandwidth selection: kernel, bandwidth type and criterion

In sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.3, the fixed and the adaptive bandwidth were selected by CV with a
Gaussian kernel. In section 3.3.4, the resulting models were compared by AICc. Slides 32 to 35 list
five kernels, fixed and adaptive bandwidths, and two criteria.

The kernel and the bandwidth determine how much each local regression smooths the data, and the
criterion determines which bandwidth is chosen:

- **Bandwidth.** A small bandwidth includes few transactions in each local regression, so the
  estimates have high variance. A large bandwidth gives estimates with low variance that average
  over local differences.
- **Criterion.** CV measures a bandwidth by the prediction error for each left-out transaction. AICc
  measures a bandwidth by the fit of the model, with a penalty for the effective number of
  parameters (slide 35).
- **Kernel.** A Gaussian kernel assigns every transaction a positive weight. A bisquare kernel
  assigns zero weight beyond the bandwidth, so with an adaptive bandwidth of $k$, exactly $k$
  transactions are used in each local regression (slide 32).

Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1996, section 3) present the Gaussian and bisquare kernels and
the CV score. Gollini et al. (2015, p. 19) describe CV and AIC as the two criteria, and write that
"in practice, a corrected version of the AIC is used". The question for this section is how the
bandwidth, the fit and the local coefficients change across the eight combinations, on the chapter's
model in dollars.

```{r}
#| results: hide
bw_grid <- expand_grid(kernel = c("gaussian", "bisquare"),
                       adaptive = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                       approach = c("CV", "AICc")) |>
  mutate(bw = pmap_dbl(list(kernel, adaptive, approach), \(k, a, ap)
    bw.gwr(f_dollar, data = condo_gw, approach = ap, kernel = k, adaptive = a)))

bw_grid <- bw_grid |>
  mutate(fit = pmap(list(kernel, adaptive, bw), \(k, a, b)
    gwr.basic(f_dollar, data = condo_gw, bw = b, kernel = k, adaptive = a)),
    AICc = map_dbl(fit, \(g) g$GW.diagnostic$AICc),
    R2 = map_dbl(fit, \(g) g$GW.diagnostic$gw.R2),
    enp = map_dbl(fit, \(g) g$GW.diagnostic$enp),
    int_min = map_dbl(fit, \(g) min(g$SDF$Intercept)),
    int_max = map_dbl(fit, \(g) max(g$SDF$Intercept)))
```

```{r}
bw_grid |>
  transmute(Kernel = kernel,
            Bandwidth = ifelse(adaptive, "adaptive", "fixed"),
            Criterion = approach,
            Value = ifelse(adaptive, paste(bw, "neighbours"), paste(round(bw), "m")),
            AICc, `R²` = R2, `Effective parameters` = enp,
            `Intercept, min ($M)` = int_min / 1e6, `Intercept, max ($M)` = int_max / 1e6) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 0, 1, 1), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
bg <- \(k, a, ap, col) bw_grid[[col]][bw_grid$kernel == k & bw_grid$adaptive == a & bw_grid$approach == ap]
best <- bw_grid |> slice_min(AICc)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
expand_grid(...)                                          # tidyr
pmap_dbl(.l, .f), pmap(.l, .f), map_dbl(.x, .f)           # purrr
```

- `expand_grid()` builds the eight combinations of kernel, bandwidth type and criterion, one row
  each.
- `pmap_dbl()` runs `bw.gwr()` once for each row with the three values of that row. `pmap()` then
  fits `gwr.basic()` with the selected bandwidth. The fitted models are kept in the list column
  `fit`. `map_dbl()` extracts one number from each model.
:::

- **Bandwidth by criterion.** With the Gaussian kernel, the bandwidth that minimises AICc
  is `r round(bg("gaussian", FALSE, "AICc", "bw"))` m (fixed)
  and `r bg("gaussian", TRUE, "AICc", "bw")` neighbours (adaptive),
  against `r round(bg("gaussian", FALSE, "CV", "bw"))` m and `r bg("gaussian", TRUE, "CV", "bw")`
  neighbours for CV.
- **Bandwidth by kernel.** With AICc, the bandwidth of the bisquare kernel
  is `r round(bg("bisquare", FALSE, "AICc", "bw") / 1000, 1)` km (fixed)
  or `r bg("bisquare", TRUE, "AICc", "bw")` neighbours (adaptive),
  against `r round(bg("gaussian", FALSE, "AICc", "bw") / 1000, 1)` km
  and `r bg("gaussian", TRUE, "AICc", "bw")` neighbours for the Gaussian kernel. The bisquare kernel
  assigns zero weight beyond the bandwidth. The Gaussian kernel assigns a positive weight to every
  transaction.
- **AICc by bandwidth type.** For the Gaussian and the bisquare kernel, the adaptive models have a
  lower AICc than the fixed-bandwidth models. The lowest AICc of the eight
  combinations, `r format(round(best$AICc), big.mark = ",")`, is for the `r best$kernel` kernel with
  an adaptive bandwidth of `r best$bw` neighbours selected by `r best$approach`. The Gaussian
  adaptive model selected by CV (section 3.3.3) has an AICc
  of `r format(round(bg("gaussian", TRUE, "CV", "AICc")), big.mark = ",")`.
- **Local intercepts by setting.** The local intercepts stay within about ±5 million dollars only
  for the fixed bandwidths chosen by AICc:
  from `r round(bg("gaussian", FALSE, "AICc", "int_min") / 1e6, 1)`
  to `r round(bg("gaussian", FALSE, "AICc", "int_max") / 1e6, 1)` million with the Gaussian kernel
  and from `r round(bg("bisquare", FALSE, "AICc", "int_min") / 1e6, 1)`
  to `r round(bg("bisquare", FALSE, "AICc", "int_max") / 1e6, 1)` million with the bisquare kernel.
  At the fixed bandwidths selected by CV and at the four adaptive bandwidths, the local intercepts
  reach tens or hundreds of millions of dollars.

## Local collinearity: correlations, VIFs, VDPs and condition numbers

In section 3.3.4, the local intercepts went down to `r round(min(gwr.adaptive$SDF$Intercept) / 1e6)`
million dollars. In section 4.3, such values appeared at six of the eight settings. The condition
number mentioned in the chapter's text is never computed (section 3.3.5). In section 3.2.6, the
largest VIF of the global model was `r round(max(mlr.vif$VIF), 2)`.

Gollini et al. (2015, section 7) explain why collinearity arises in GWR when the global model has
none:

- each local regression uses a small, heavily weighted sample, in which two variables can be closely
  related even if they are unrelated across Singapore;
- a variable that hardly varies within a neighbourhood becomes collinear with the intercept, because
  the variable and the intercept column are then almost constant in the local sample.

Gollini et al. (2015) add that in the presence of collinearity, GWR "may find patterns in the
coefficients where no patterns are actually present". Their rules of thumb for local collinearity
are an absolute local correlation above 0.8, a local VIF above 10, a variance decomposition
proportion (VDP) above 0.5, or a local condition number above 30. Lu et al. (2014, section 5.2)
apply them with `gwr.collin.diagno()`. The question for this section is whether the chapter's
adaptive model is locally collinear, where, and through which variables.

```{r}
collin <- gwr.collin.diagno(f_dollar, data = condo_gw, bw = bw.adaptive,
                            kernel = "gaussian", adaptive = TRUE)

belsley_cn <- function(X) {
  Xs <- sweep(X, 2, sqrt(colSums(X^2)), "/")
  d <- svd(Xs)$d
  max(d) / min(d)
}
X_global <- cbind(Intercept = 1, as.matrix(st_drop_geometry(condo_gw)[x_vars]))
global_cn <- belsley_cn(X_global)
global_cn
summary(collin$local_CN)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
gwr.collin.diagno(formula, data, bw, kernel, adaptive)    # GWmodel
svd(x)                                                    # base R
```

- `gwr.collin.diagno()` computes, at each transaction and with the same weights as the GWR, the
  local correlation of every pair of variables, the local VIFs, the VDPs and the condition number.
- `belsley_cn()` computes the condition number of the global model. Each column of the design
  matrix, the intercept included, is scaled to length 1, and the condition number is the largest
  singular value divided by the smallest singular value.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
cn <- collin$local_CN
vdp <- as.data.frame(collin$SDF) |> select(ends_with("_VDP"))
top_cn <- order(cn, decreasing = TRUE)[1:50]
vdp_top <- sort(colMeans(vdp[top_cn, ]), decreasing = TRUE)
xy_gw <- st_coordinates(condo_gw)
nn30 <- FNN::get.knn(xy_gw, k = 29)$nn.index
cbd_local_cv <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(condo_gw)), \(i) {
  v <- condo_gw$PROX_CBD[c(i, nn30[i, ])]
  sd(v) / mean(v)
})
cbd_global_cv <- sd(condo_gw$PROX_CBD) / mean(condo_gw$PROX_CBD)
int_top <- abs(gwr.adaptive$SDF$Intercept) > quantile(abs(gwr.adaptive$SDF$Intercept), 0.95)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(mutate(condo_gw, local_CN = cn)) +
  tm_dots(fill = "local_CN", size = 0.3,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(breaks = c(0, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 10000, Inf),
                                          values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local condition number")) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
```

- **Global condition number.** The condition number of the global model is `r round(global_cn, 1)`,
  below 30.
- **Local condition numbers.** The local condition number is above 30 at `r sum(cn > 30)` of the
  1,436 transactions, above 300 at `r sum(cn > 300)` transactions, and above 1,000
  at `r sum(cn > 1000)` transactions. The median local condition number is `r round(median(cn))` and
  the maximum is `r format(round(max(cn)), big.mark = ",")`.
- **Condition number by intercept size.** For the 5% of transactions with the largest local
  intercepts, the median local condition number
  is `r format(round(median(cn[int_top])), big.mark = ",")`, against `r round(median(cn[!int_top]))`
  for the other 95% of transactions.
- **Collinearity with the intercept.** For the 50 transactions with the highest condition numbers,
  the mean VDP on the largest condition index is `r round(vdp_top[1], 2)`
  for `r sub("_VDP", "", names(vdp_top)[1])`, `r round(vdp_top[2], 2)`
  for `r sub("_VDP", "", names(vdp_top)[2])` and `r round(vdp_top[3], 2)`
  for `r sub("_VDP", "", names(vdp_top)[3])`, each above 0.5. `PROX_CBD` illustrates the case of
  Gollini et al. in which a variable hardly varies within a neighbourhood: its coefficient of
  variation is `r round(cbd_global_cv, 2)` across Singapore, and its median among the 30 nearest
  neighbours of a transaction is `r round(median(cbd_local_cv), 3)`. Locally, distance to the CBD is
  almost constant, and its coefficient is collinear with the intercept.

The intercept of −135 million dollars in section 3.3.4 and the intercepts of −150 million dollars on
slide 38 are therefore consistent with local collinearity. These intercepts are unlikely to reflect
actual prices. The remedies listed by Gollini et al. are to do nothing, to remove a variable, to
transform the variables, or to use a GWR designed for collinearity, such as GW ridge regression.
`PROX_CBD` is retained, because it has the largest |t| among the locational variables of the global
model, `r round(abs(summary(condo.mlr1)$coefficients["PROX_CBD", "t value"]), 1)`. In section 4.5, a
bisquare kernel with an adaptive bandwidth chosen by AICc is used.

## Model comparison: OLS and GWR in dollars and in logs

Matthews and Yang (2012, p. 154) write that researchers "typically use the Akaike Information
Criterion (AIC)" to compare "a 'global' OLS linear regression model with those from the local GWR
model". The model in this section differs from the chapter's in two choices supported by sections
4.1 to 4.4: the price is in logs, and the bandwidth is chosen by AICc. The kernel follows from
section 4.3, where the adaptive bisquare kernel has the lowest AICc. The question for this section
is how the four models compare: OLS and GWR, in dollars and in logs.

```{r}
#| results: hide
bw.log <- bw.gwr(f_log, data = condo_gw, approach = "AICc",
                 kernel = "bisquare", adaptive = TRUE)
gwr.log <- gwr.basic(f_log, data = condo_gw, bw = bw.log,
                     kernel = "bisquare", adaptive = TRUE)
collin.log <- gwr.collin.diagno(f_log, data = condo_gw, bw = bw.log,
                                kernel = "bisquare", adaptive = TRUE)
```

```{r}
lm_aicc_of <- function(m) {
  k <- length(coef(m)) + 1
  AIC(m) + 2 * k * (k + 1) / (nobs(m) - k - 1)
}
moran_of <- function(r) moran.test(r, lw_1500)$estimate[[1]]

tibble(
  Model = c("OLS", "GWR, adaptive Gaussian, k = 30, CV", "OLS",
            paste0("GWR, adaptive bisquare, k = ", bw.log, ", AICc")),
  Response = c("dollars", "dollars", "logs", "logs"),
  AICc = c(lm_aicc_of(condo.mlr1), gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$AICc,
           lm_aicc_of(condo.mlr1.log), gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$AICc),
  `R²` = c(summary(condo.mlr1)$r.squared, gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$gw.R2,
           summary(condo.mlr1.log)$r.squared, gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$gw.R2),
  `Residual Moran's I` = c(moran_of(residuals(condo.mlr1)), moran_of(gwr.adaptive$SDF$residual),
                           moran_of(residuals(condo.mlr1.log)), moran_of(gwr.log$SDF$residual)),
  `Median local CN` = c(NA, median(collin$local_CN), NA, median(collin.log$local_CN))) |>
  mutate(`Median local CN` = ifelse(is.na(`Median local CN`), "n/a",
                                    format(round(`Median local CN`)))) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 1, 3, 3, 0), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `lm_aicc_of()` computes the AICc of an `lm` model with the correction of slide 35, counting the
  residual variance as a parameter. For `condo.mlr1` it returns the global AICc printed by
  `gwr.basic()` in section 3.3.2.
- `moran_of()` returns Moran's I of a set of residuals, with the 1,500 m weights of section 4.2.
- AICc values are comparable only between models with the same response variable, dollars or logs.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
cl_log <- as.data.frame(st_drop_geometry(gwr.log$SDF))
int_rng_log <- range(cl_log$Intercept)
mrt_rng_log <- range(pct(cl_log$PROX_MRT))
```

- **GWR improves on OLS in dollars and in logs.** The AICc falls
  by `r format(round(lm_aicc_of(condo.mlr1) - gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$AICc), big.mark = ",")` in
  dollars and by `r round(lm_aicc_of(condo.mlr1.log) - gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$AICc)` in logs.
- **GWR removes the spatial autocorrelation of the residuals.** Moran's I of the residuals falls
  from 0.14 (OLS, dollars) and 0.20 (OLS, logs) to −0.02 and −0.03 for GWR in dollars and in logs,
  which is consistent with the local coefficients absorbing the location effect.
- **The log model's local coefficients.** The local intercepts range
  from `r round(int_rng_log[1], 1)` to `r round(int_rng_log[2], 1)` in logs. The local effect of
  each additional kilometre from the MRT ranges from `r round(mrt_rng_log[1])`%
  to `r round(mrt_rng_log[2])`%. The local condition numbers are higher than for the chapter's model
  (median `r round(median(collin.log$local_CN))` against `r round(median(collin$local_CN))`), so the
  extreme local coefficients may reflect collinearity.

## Spatial non-stationarity: pseudo-F and Monte Carlo tests

In the chapter, the lower AICc of GWR in section 3.3.2 is called "significantly smaller". According
to slide 29, spatial non-stationarity "is assumed and will be tested". The readings describe a test
of the whole model and a test of each coefficient:

- **Overall improvement of GWR over OLS.** Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1999) compare the
  residual sums of squares of OLS and GWR in an ANOVA table (their Table 2). The reduction in
  residual sum of squares from OLS to GWR is divided by its degrees of freedom and compared with the
  GWR residual variance. The ratio is the pseudo-F statistic.
- **Variation of each coefficient.** Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton (1996, section 3) permute
  the transactions among the locations, refit the GWR, and compare the variation of each coefficient
  with its variation in the permuted data. If prices do not depend on location, every permutation is
  as likely as the real arrangement. The bandwidth selected for the real data is reused for every
  permutation, a shortcut permitted in the 1996 paper. Lu et al. (2014, section 4.2) describe the
  test as implemented in `gwr.montecarlo()`.

The question for this section is whether the local model on the log scale is a significant
improvement, and which of its 15 coefficients vary significantly over Singapore.

```{r}
rss_ols <- sum(residuals(condo.mlr1.log)^2)
rss_gwr <- gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$RSS.gw
df_ols <- df.residual(condo.mlr1.log)
df_gwr <- gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$edf
anova_gwr <- tibble(
  Source = c("OLS residuals", "GWR improvement", "GWR residuals"),
  SS = c(rss_ols, rss_ols - rss_gwr, rss_gwr),
  df = c(df_ols, df_ols - df_gwr, df_gwr)) |>
  mutate(MS = SS / df)
F_gwr <- anova_gwr$MS[2] / anova_gwr$MS[3]
p_F <- pf(F_gwr, anova_gwr$df[2], anova_gwr$df[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
kable(anova_gwr, digits = c(0, 2, 1, 4))
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1234)
mc_test <- gwr.montecarlo(f_log, data = condo_gw, nsims = 99,
                          kernel = "bisquare", adaptive = TRUE, bw = bw.log)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# The loop of gwr.montecarlo(), run on several cores. Each permutation is applied to the
# previous one, as in the function, so the permutations are drawn first, in the same order.
gwr_montecarlo_par <- function(formula, data, nsims, kernel, adaptive, bw) {
  d0 <- gw.dist(st_coordinates(data))
  mf <- model.frame(formula, st_drop_geometry(data))
  y <- model.response(mf)
  x <- model.matrix(attr(mf, "terms"), mf)
  n <- length(y)
  perms <- list(seq_len(n))
  for (k in seq_len(nsims)) perms[[k + 1]] <- perms[[k]][order(sample(n))]
  v <- do.call(rbind, parallel::mclapply(perms, \(pm) {
    dm <- d0[pm, pm]
    b <- t(sapply(seq_len(n), \(i)
      GWmodel:::gw_reg_2(x, y, gw.weight(dm[, i], bw, kernel, adaptive))))
    apply(b, 2, var)
  }, mc.cores = max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 2)))
  p <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(v)), \(j)
    1 - which(sort(v[, j], index.return = TRUE)$ix == 1) / (nsims + 1))
  matrix(p, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(colnames(x), "p-value"))
}
set.seed(1234)
mc_test <- gwr_montecarlo_par(f_log, condo_gw, nsims = 99, kernel = "bisquare",
                              adaptive = TRUE, bw = bw.log)
```

```{r}
mc_tbl <- tibble(Coefficient = rownames(mc_test), `p-value` = mc_test[, 1]) |>
  arrange(`p-value`)
kable(mc_tbl, digits = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
gwr.montecarlo(formula, data, nsims, kernel, adaptive, bw) # GWmodel
pf(q, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)                       # stats
```

- The ANOVA uses the residual sums of squares of `condo.mlr1.log` and `gwr.log`, and the residual
  degrees of freedom of each. For GWR, the residual degrees of freedom are `edf`, $n -
  2\,\mathrm{tr}(S) + \mathrm{tr}(S^\top S)$, printed by `gwr.basic()`. This ANOVA is the simplest
  form of the test: Brunsdon et al. (1999) refine the degrees of freedom with a further
  approximation.
- `gwr.montecarlo()` permutes the rows among the locations 99 times, the default of the function,
  and refits the GWR each time with `bw.log`. For each coefficient, it returns the share of the 100
  data sets, 99 permuted and the real one, in which the local values vary at least as much as in the
  real data.
- `gwr.montecarlo()` fits the 143,600 local regressions one after another, which takes about 35
  minutes. The page runs the same loop on several cores. The permutations are drawn in the same
  order after `set.seed(1234)`, so the p-values are those of `gwr.montecarlo()`. The two gave the
  same p-values in a test with 3 permutations.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
mc_sig <- mc_tbl$Coefficient[mc_tbl$`p-value` < 0.05]
mc_ns <- mc_tbl$Coefficient[mc_tbl$`p-value` >= 0.05]
```

The pseudo-F statistic is `r round(F_gwr, 2)` on `r round(anova_gwr$df[2], 1)`
and `r round(anova_gwr$df[3], 1)` degrees of freedom
(p `r ifelse(p_F < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("=", signif(p_F, 2)))`), so GWR is a significant
improvement on OLS. In the Monte Carlo test, `r length(mc_sig)` of the 15 coefficients vary
significantly at the 5% level: `r paste0("\x60", mc_sig, "\x60", collapse = ", ")`. For the
other `r length(mc_ns)` coefficients, `r paste0("\x60", mc_ns, "\x60", collapse = ", ")`, the
variation of the local values does not exceed the variation in the permuted data at the 5% level. A
single global coefficient may be sufficient for each of them. Brunsdon et al. (1999, sections 4
and 5) call a model with some coefficients global and others local a mixed GWR.

## Coefficient maps: local significance after a multiple-test adjustment

The maps of section 3.3.7 show the standard error and the t-value of the floor-area coefficient,
without the coefficient itself. The outline lists two references on maps of GWR coefficients, Mennis
(2006) and Matthews and Yang (2012).

Mennis (2006) describes problems in published GWR maps:

- the coefficients are shown without their t-values, a practice that "may visually emphasize the
  areas of highest (or lowest ...) parameter estimation, regardless of the significance of the
  estimate";
- the classes have equal width and the colours are of a single hue, so the map hides the sign of the
  coefficient.

Mennis recommends a diverging colour scheme centred on zero.

Matthews and Yang (2012) show the coefficient on one map only where its local t-value is beyond
±1.96, significant at the 5% level.

With 1,436 local tests per coefficient, about 72 tests would be "significant" at 5% by chance alone,
even if the coefficient were zero everywhere. Lu et al. (2014, section 5.1) describe four
adjustments for multiple local tests. Byrne, Charlton and Fotheringham (2009) propose one of these
adjustments, designed for GWR, and Matthews and Yang (2012) cite it. Neighbouring regressions share
their data, so the local tests are correlated. The adjustment replaces the number of tests with the
effective number of parameters $p_e$ (Lu et al., 2014, equation 15):

$$\alpha = \frac{0.05}{1 + p_e - p_e / p}$$

where $\alpha$ is the adjusted significance level and $p = 15$ is the number of coefficients of each
local regression. The question for this section is at which locations the coefficients that vary
significantly (section 4.6) still have a significant local t-value after this adjustment.

```{r}
#| echo: false
enp_log <- gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$enp
alpha_fb <- 0.05 / (1 + enp_log - enp_log / 15)
```

The adjusted level is $\alpha$ = `r format(signif(alpha_fb, 2), scientific = FALSE)`, so a local |t|
above `r round(qt(1 - alpha_fb / 2, gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$edf), 2)` is significant.

```{r}
gwr_log_sf <- gwr.log$SDF |>
  mutate(across(all_of(x_vars), \(b) 100 * (exp(b) - 1), .names = "{.col}_PCT"))

coef_map <- function(var, unit) {
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha_fb / 2, gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$edf)
  dat <- gwr_log_sf |>
    mutate(value = ifelse(abs(.data[[paste0(var, "_TV")]]) > t_crit,
                          .data[[paste0(var, "_PCT")]], NA))
  tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey80", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(dat) +
    tm_dots(fill = "value", size = 0.25,
            fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 6, style = "pretty", midpoint = 0,
                                            values = "brewer.rd_bu",
                                            value.na = "grey60", label.na = "not significant"),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = unit)) +
    tm_title(var)
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `across(..., .names = "{.col}_PCT")` adds, for each variable, the local coefficient as a
  percentage effect on the price, $100(e^b - 1)$.
- `coef_map()` keeps the percentage where the local |t| is above the adjusted critical value and
  sets it to `NA` elsewhere. Transactions with `NA` are drawn in grey.
- `midpoint = 0` with the diverging red-blue palette puts zero at the neutral colour, so that blue
  and red show the sign of the effect, as Mennis (2006) recommends.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8.5
mapped_vars <- intersect(c("AREA_SQM", "AGE", "PROX_CBD", "PROX_MRT", "FREEHOLD", "PROX_PARK"),
                         mc_sig)
units <- c(AREA_SQM = "% per m²", AGE = "% per year", PROX_CBD = "% per km",
           PROX_MRT = "% per km", FREEHOLD = "% for freehold", PROX_PARK = "% per km")
tmap_arrange(map(mapped_vars, \(v) coef_map(v, units[[v]])), ncol = 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha_fb / 2, gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$edf)
sig_share <- sapply(x_vars, \(v) c(
  raw = mean(abs(gwr_log_sf[[paste0(v, "_TV")]]) > 1.96),
  adjusted = mean(abs(gwr_log_sf[[paste0(v, "_TV")]]) > t_crit)))
sig_tbl <- tibble(Coefficient = x_vars,
                  `Monte Carlo p` = mc_test[x_vars, 1],
                  `Share significant, |t| > 1.96` = sig_share["raw", ],
                  `Share significant, adjusted` = sig_share["adjusted", ])
```

```{r}
kable(sig_tbl, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
sig_areas <- st_join(gwr_log_sf, mpsz_svy21[, "PLN_AREA_N"]) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
area_summary <- function(v) {
  sig_areas |>
    mutate(pc = .data[[paste0(v, "_PCT")]], sig = abs(.data[[paste0(v, "_TV")]]) > t_crit) |>
    filter(sig) |>
    group_by(PLN_AREA_N) |>
    summarise(n = n(), median_pc = median(pc), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(n))
}
area_med <- \(v, a) round(area_summary(v)$median_pc[area_summary(v)$PLN_AREA_N == a])
n_sig <- \(v) sum(abs(gwr_log_sf[[paste0(v, "_TV")]]) > t_crit)
adj_share <- sig_tbl[["Share significant, adjusted"]]
share_area <- round(100 * adj_share[sig_tbl$Coefficient == "AREA_SQM"])
share_min <- round(100 * min(adj_share[sig_tbl$Coefficient != "AREA_SQM"]))
share_max <- round(100 * max(adj_share[sig_tbl$Coefficient != "AREA_SQM"]))
```

After the adjustment, only floor area is significant almost everywhere, at `r share_area`% of the
transactions, with a local effect of 0.2% to 0.6% per square metre. The Monte Carlo p-value of floor
area, `r round(mc_test["AREA_SQM", 1], 2)`, is consistent with variation no larger than in permuted
data. A single global coefficient of 0.48% per square metre (section 4.1) may therefore be
sufficient. The coefficients that do vary are significant only in parts of the island,
at `r share_min`% to `r share_max`% of the transactions. Without the adjustment, the share of
significant transactions for each coefficient that varies is about three times as large or more.

On the four maps:

- **`FREEHOLD`** is significant at `r n_sig("FREEHOLD")` transactions, all positive. The median
  freehold premium is `r area_med("FREEHOLD", "TANGLIN")`% in
  Tanglin, `r area_med("FREEHOLD", "RIVER VALLEY")`% in River Valley
  and `r area_med("FREEHOLD", "BUKIT MERAH")`% in Bukit Merah, against the
  global `r round(pct(cl["FREEHOLD"]))`% of section 4.1, and `r area_med("FREEHOLD", "BEDOK")`% in
  Bedok. The premium is largest in the central area. The Central Region
  contains `r sum(condo_pa$FREEHOLD == 1 & condo_pa$REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")` of
  the `r sum(condo_pa$FREEHOLD == 1)` freehold units in the data.
- **`PROX_MRT`** is significant at `r n_sig("PROX_MRT")` transactions, almost all negative, in
  Novena, Tanglin, River Valley, Newton and Clementi. There, each additional kilometre from a
  station is associated with a price about half as high (median `r area_med("PROX_MRT", "NOVENA")`%
  in Novena), against `r round(pct(cl["PROX_MRT"]))`% globally.
- **`PROX_CBD`** is significant at `r n_sig("PROX_CBD")` transactions. In the east the coefficient
  is negative, a median of `r area_med("PROX_CBD", "BEDOK")`% per kilometre in Bedok. In Clementi
  the coefficient is positive, a median of `r area_med("PROX_CBD", "CLEMENTI")`% per kilometre. A
  price that nearly triples with each kilometre from the CBD is unlikely to reflect distance alone.
  Clementi is also the area where `PROX_MRT` has its largest negative effect. The local collinearity
  described in section 4.4 may account for the positive `PROX_CBD` and the large negative `PROX_MRT`
  coefficients there.
- **`PROX_PARK`** is significant at `r n_sig("PROX_PARK")` transactions, positive in Bedok and
  negative in Clementi, Tampines and Bukit Timah. The global coefficient of section 4.1 averages
  these opposite local effects.

On the maps, the question of slide 4, why central units sold for more, is answered only in part. The
freehold premium and the price decrease per kilometre from an MRT station are larger in the central
area than elsewhere. The larger central effects may be one reason central units sell for more. The
effect of floor area does not vary significantly across the island.

# Reflection

The aim of chapter 13 is to explain why some condominium units sold for more than others, and why
central units sold for more. On this page, the effect of the same features on the price differs by
location, with qualifications that the chapter does not raise.

**Log scale of the price.** The chapter computes the log of the price, and its models use the price
in dollars. In dollars, the residuals are skewed, heavy-tailed, U-shaped against the fitted price
and more spread out for expensive units. In logs, the U-shape and the long upper tail are no longer
present, and the spread remains. Each coefficient is then a percentage effect, the measure a buyer
uses to compare a unit of 1 million dollars with a unit of 5 million dollars.

**Local collinearity.** An intercept of −135 million dollars, or a fall of 44 million dollars per
kilometre from an MRT station, occurs where the local condition number is highest. Within a
neighbourhood of 30 transactions, the median coefficient of variation of distance to the CBD
is `r round(median(cbd_local_cv), 3)`, and that variable is collinear with the intercept. The local
condition numbers have a median of `r round(median(cn))` and
reach `r format(round(max(cn)), big.mark = ",")`, against the threshold of 30 of Gollini et al.
(2015). Slide 38 shows intercepts down to −150 million dollars. A wider bisquare kernel on the log
scale narrows the range of most coefficients. Every local model remains more collinear than the
global model. In Clementi, distance to the CBD still has a median effect of about +200% per
kilometre.

**Variation of the coefficients.** In the Monte Carlo test of Brunsdon, Fotheringham and Charlton
(1996), `r length(mc_sig)` of the 15 coefficients vary significantly at the 5% level. A mixed GWR
(Brunsdon et al., 1999) could give floor area and age a single global coefficient.

**Adjusted significance threshold.** With 1,436 local tests per coefficient, the adjustment of
Byrne, Charlton and Fotheringham (2009) raises the critical |t| from about 1.96 for a single test to
about `r round(qt(1 - alpha_fb / 2, gwr.log$GW.diagnostic$edf), 1)`.

As in chapters 9 to 12, four steps in the chapter ran without error and without the effect described
in the surrounding text:

- `LOG_SELLING_PRICE` was computed, and every model in the chapter uses `SELLING_PRICE`;
- the GWR maps were written with `eval: false` in `tmap` 3 syntax, so no map of the GWR results
  appears on the chapter's page;
- `global_moran_perm()` returned a p-value of 0, printed as "< 2.2e-16";
- the condition number was described from the ArcGIS help page "Interpreting GWR results", and the
  chapter computes no condition number from the data.

**Limits.** The data are one year of resales, 2015. Heteroscedasticity remains on the log scale.
Floor level, view and developer are missing from the model, and their omission may account for part
of the lower local R² in the Central Region (section 3.3.6). Mixed GWR and GW ridge regression, the
remedies described in the readings for global coefficients and local collinearity, are not fitted
here.
